item.title: REVIEW: IDX Complete identity theft protection review
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
A cost-effective cybersecurity software bundle for individuals and families, but some improvements are needed. Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. Individual cybersecurity could previously be glossed over, but the situation has changed. Cyber threats have become more sophisticated, as malicious actors increasingly deploy artificial intelligence (AI) tools. From AI-generated phishing emails to deepfakes and automated vulnerability scanning, individuals need protection against the widening net of cyberattacks. The good thing is that AI also aids in fighting cyberattacks. Cybersecurity tools have become much more sophisticated at countering sneaky methods. To make online protection more accessible, platforms offer all-in-one cybersecurity suites with many features. IDX is one example, and I’m reviewing it to see how it stacks up alongside the best data removal services and identity theft protection tools we've tested. Read on to learn about the features you’ll get with an IDX Complete subscription, its pros & cons, and how it fares against competitors. You can see the full list of services from IDX by clicking here. IDX offers various pricing plans, but in this review I’m focusing on the Complete bundle. For $33 monthly, this bundle offers a data removal service, password manager, VPN, dark web monitoring, identity theft insurance, and many other features. It's a steal compared to paying for each feature separately. Think of having to pay separately for a VPN, password manager, and data removal platform– it can run into $100 a month, compared to a $33-per-month IDX Complete plan. Users who pay annually get a 10% discount compared to paying month-to-month. I’m unimpressed with this discount, as 30% to 50% is the norm for most cybersecurity bundles I’ve reviewed. If I decide to pay for 12 months upfront, I think I deserve more than 10% off, but some platforms disagree. IDX also offers a family version of the Complete plan. For $65 per month, the same features on the individual plan are expanded to 2 adults and 5 dependents under 18. It’s built for a conventional family of two parents and several children. I’ve reviewed many family cybersecurity bundles and hardly encountered age specifications for users. It’s usually just a limit (e.g., 5 or 10 members) regardless of age, but IDX Complete is the exception. IDX doesn’t offer a standard free trial or money-back guarantee. This is another complaint I have about its pricing system. Setting up IDX follows a straightforward pattern. It starts by entering your name and email, then choosing a password. However, there’s an obstacle here. I mentioned that IDX doesn’t offer a free trial—users have to choose a plan and enter payment details before gaining access. It’s a strictly paywalled service, unlike several platforms I’ve tested that offered free trials at the get-go, then requested a payment later. After subscribing to the IDX Complete bundle and gaining access, it’s time to start using its security features. IDX offers many features under this bundle, so much that I’ll struggle to cover every one in this review. Instead, I’ll focus on the core features that keep users safe online. The first is the ForgetMe data removal service. With this feature, you can scan data broker sites for your personal information. If your information is found on any site, IDX sends automated deletion requests. An IDX scan covers 100+ data broker sites, which isn’t as extensive as designated data removal platforms (many rivals cover 500+ sites), but it’s sufficient to remove your information from the most popular data broker sites. The second is the password manager. This tool lets you store passwords securely and, if needed, share them with others. When it’s time to log into any site with a saved password, you’ll simply autofill the details. This tool also checks if your password got compromised in data breach incidents and alerts you immediately– the corrective action is to change the password for every site where you’ve used it. The third is the virtual private network (VPN) feature. A VPN encrypts your online traffic by routing it through remote servers—think of surfing the web in the U.K., but using an IP address from faraway Australia. Your identity gets disguised to third parties that want to show you personalized ads or maybe stage malicious attacks. A VPN is particularly important when you use public WiFi networks, which are often insecure. When using the IDX VPN, I could choose from roughly 20 server locations. This figure pales compared to dedicated VPN apps, some of which offer 200+ locations from countries down to cities. IDX’s server coverage is nowhere near as widespread, but the VPN worked reliably. For U.S.-based users, IDX Complete includes identity theft recovery and insurance. That is, if a user experiences identity theft, IDX experts walk them through the corrective actions (e.g., freezing credit files and closing certain accounts). Users can get reimbursed for damages if they pay for an insurance plan. Admittedly, I didn’t get to test the identity theft recovery feature (and hopefully won’t need it soon), but it’s a valuable service when needed. From my perspective, IDX Complete doesn’t offer the best of each feature, relative to competitors, but the bundle is unbeatable. It’s not the best VPN compared to standalone VPN apps, nor the best data removal platform compared to rivals. However, offering many cybersecurity features in one cost-effective package is the selling point. IDX offers a modern interface that I liked using. It’s best described as minimal and simple. It’s not too interactive like I’ve found on some apps, yet not too bland. I’ll say it prioritized function over form, with features neatly arranged in places users can easily find them. You can access IDX from a web browser or download the mobile app (iOS and Android). I’ve tested various cybersecurity tools that didn’t have mobile apps, so I’ll note that having both iOS and Android apps is a benefit. Given its numerous features, IDX Complete is a highly effective privacy protection tool. With it, you get to kill multiple cybersecurity-related birds with one stone. Better still, you get the numerous features at a lower cost in one bundle compared to paying for each one separately. IDX users get decent support resources, starting with a Knowledge Center offering detailed user guides, how-tos, and articles discussing emerging cyber threats to watch out for. There’s also an FAQs section that provides solutions to frequently encountered issues. For direct support, users can contact IDX’s staff by filling out an online ticket, and a response is delivered via email. Competition is the name of the game in the cybersecurity niche, with countless platforms offering all-in-one bundles similar to IDX Complete. The PrivacyHawk bundle is the most notable rival I’ll mention. It offers similar personal protection features at an affordable price: $30 per month for the most advanced plan, which includes identity theft protection, dark web monitoring, data removal, and spam filtering. Personally, I prefer PrivacyHawk because it offers some free scans to help users test its features, unlike IDX, which requires payment before granting access. PrivacyHawk also has a 30-day money-back guarantee, which IDX doesn’t offer. IDX Complete provides much value for money. For a monthly subscription, you’ll unlock various tools to protect your online privacy, getting a good deal compared to paying for each tool independently. However, I think IDX should offer a standard free trial to attract users. Being hard-paywalled puts it at a competitive disadvantage.

item.title: REVIEW: Fitbit Edge Review: A Stylish Fitness Tracker With Enhanced Features
item.description:
Source: Engadget, PCMag
The Fitbit Edge positions itself as a modern fitness tracker with a focus on design and usability, offering a balance between traditional activity tracking and smartwatch-like functionality. Priced at $179.99, it succeeds the 2023 Charge 6 with a vibrant 1.34-inch AMOLED display, glanceable metrics, and features like media controls and turn-by-turn directions. While it lacks NFC payments and battery stamina that would set records, its strong sleep tracking and integration with Google Health keep it competitive. The Edge sits between the $99 Fitbit Air and the $399 Pixel Watch 5 in Google's wearable lineup, bridging the gap between screenless trackers and full smartwatches. Its design, described as a 'curvier and wider oblong' compared to previous models like the Luxe and Alta, features a bright, navigable touchscreen and an updated feature set that makes it feel more modern. The display, covered in durable Gorilla Glass, is consistently bright and easy to read in various lighting conditions, though occasional lag was noted when the device was in sleep mode. The Edge's touchscreen, while responsive enough for basic navigation, is not as feature-rich as Wear OS platforms, with preloaded apps limited to essentials like Alarm, ECG, and Weather. Users can customize clock faces and widgets to display preferred metrics, though the screen is intended for quick glances rather than complex interactions. The device also includes standalone GPS for phone-free pace and route tracking, an altimeter for floor tracking, and a user-replaceable battery. While it cannot access Gemini or download third-party apps like the Pixel Watch 5, its seamless compatibility with both iOS and Android devices sets it apart. The Fitbit Edge is praised for its sleek appearance, practical design, and improved functionality over earlier models, earning it an Editors' Choice award for traditional fitness trackers with a screen. However, its limited app ecosystem and absence of NFC support may deter some users seeking more advanced features.

item.title: REVIEW: Sony WH-1000XM4C Review: A Familiar Favorite, Still With Superb Sound
item.description:
Source: PCMag
Sony is bringing back a legend. The Sony WH-1000XM4 headphones were some of the most beloved in the series. With prices of newer models rising, it seems Sony is ready to bring them back, and for less cash. The Sony WH-1000XM4C headphones aren't an exact reproduction of the original XM4, but they're pretty close. Even better, they are available for $299.99—$50 less than the original and $60 less than the Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) ($359), although the Bose has superior ANC and USB-C audio support. The XM4C has its own strengths, though. Ultimately, the XM4C keeps everything that made the originals great and is easy to recommend, even if it's not as capable as the higher-end, Editors' Choice Sony WH-1000XM6 ($459.99). If you owned the original XM4, the XM4C will feel immediately familiar—the headphones essentially look the same. They have the same folding, swiveling over-ear design, lightweight plastic build, and control layout. The XM5 headphones did away with the folding earcups, which saw enough criticism to bring them back for the XM6. In their carry case, the headphones are similar in footprint to the XM6, if slightly smaller. They'll fit in a bag perfectly fine. The XM4C comes in Black, Platinum Silver, and Lavender. I tested the Platinum Silver model, which has a clean, light finish. The same overall build means that they're just as comfortable, too. There's plenty of padding in the earcups and under the headband, making for a pair of headphones you can easily wear for hours and hours on end without discomfort. That has been what makes Sony headphones so ideal for travel for so long. Like the original XM4, these headphones don't have an IP rating, so you'll want to be careful with them around water. The headphones have the same touch controls as the original XM4, and they're generally responsive and easy to use. In the right earcup, double-tap to play or pause audio; swipe forward or back to skip to the next or previous track; swipe up or down to adjust volume; cover the panel to activate Quick Attention; and tap and hold to activate your voice assistant. Other controls are on the left earcup: a power button to turn the headphones on and off, and a "Custom" button that cycles through noise modes. You can customize a few things, but not a ton. For example, you can reassign the custom button to activate a voice assistant, or turn the touch panel off if you'd prefer. As you might expect, there are a few updates to the headphones, such as connectivity. While the original XM4 headphones had Bluetooth 5.0, this model upgrades to Bluetooth 6.0. They support Bluetooth Multipoint for up to two simultaneous connections and have Google Fast Pair. Inside, things are decidedly more dated. The XM4C keeps the original's 40mm drivers, HD Noise Cancelling Processor QN1, and four-microphone ANC array. For context, the XM5 uses eight microphones, and the XM6 has 12, along with the newer QN3 processor. The 3.5mm port for wired listening is retained, thankfully, along with DSEE Extreme. The headphones support AAC, SBC, and LDAC. Battery life takes a step backward compared with the original headphones. Sony rates the XM4C at up to 27 hours with ANC on and 34 hours with it off, down from the original XM4's 30-hour ANC-on rating. That's a strange trade-off for a refresh, given that the XM6 promises 30 hours with ANC and 40 hours with ANC off. It looks worse next to competitors like the JBL Live 770NC, which manages 44 hours with ANC enabled and 70 hours with it off, and the Fender Mix, which delivers a lengthy 52 hours with ANC enabled and 100 off. A three-minute quick charge gets you up to an hour of playback—well short of the XM6 and 770NC, which give you three hours from the same three minutes. The reason for the shorter battery life is pretty interesting, though. The headphones have to comply with an upcoming EU regulation around making batteries replaceable. These aren't built for you to regularly swap out the batteries; it's still an involved process, and Sony has yet to detail how to do it. But, at least when the battery starts to reach the end of its lifespan, it doesn't mean the headphones have to go in the trash. In the box, apart from the headphones and carry case, you'll also get a 3.5mm cable for wired listening. There's no USB-C cable in the box, though. The WH-1000XM4C connects to the same Sony Sound Connect app as the rest of Sony's headphone lineup, and it's reasonably well-designed and easy to use. In the app, you can easily manage noise modes, tweak controls, and more. The EQ is one of the more upgraded aspects of the app for these headphones versus the original XM4. The XM4C headphones have the same 10-band EQ as the WH-1000XM6 headphones, which makes it easier to tweak the audio response to your preferences. Bands range from 31Hz to 16kHz. The new headphones also have a new gaming EQ preset that wasn't available on the original XM4. If you've used Sony headphones recently, you're probably reasonably familiar with the SoundConnect app and will find it easy to navigate. It's definitely a whole lot better than the HeadphonesConnect app was back when the original WH-1000XM4 headphones were released. So how does six-year-old ANC hardware hold up? Better than I thought it would. The ANC on these headphones is still very, very good, and although newer options have improved ANC overall, don't expect the WH-1000XM4C to underperform. Against recorded airplane engine noise, the XM4C cut low frequencies down a lot, leaving some faint background hiss that could be easily covered up with music. Bus noise was a similar story, with the low engine rumble handled well and only some of the higher-frequency intermittent sounds sneaking through. In a busy cafe, the headphones did a pretty good job at cutting out much of the background chatter, but closer voices could be heard, even if they were in the background. I'd argue that the headphones aren't that far behind some of the best ANC today when it comes to consistent background noise like plane engines, but tech has improved a lot when it comes to cancelling out those inconsistent, random noises. That said, the ANC on these is still better than some others at a similar price. It's better than the likes of the Nothing Headphone (1), for example. Transparency mode is one area that has improved dramatically over the past few years, so newer headphones tend to have better tech. On these headphones, it's fine for quick conversations and sounds natural enough, but it's not as good as the AirPods Max 2 or the more expensive XM6. Sony says it retuned the XM4C's sound profile for "today's listening preferences," targeting clearer, richer vocals and tighter bass. That's a tuning and processing change rather than new drivers—the 40mm drivers are the same as the 2020 model. Ultimately, I really quite like how these headphones sound. The bass response is definitely a little tamer than that of some other headphones, as heard on tracks like "Silent Shout" by The Knife. This track has pretty heavy sub-bass content, and it wasn't as boomy as it can be on some consumer headphones. Don't take that to mean that it's not there, though; on the contrary, I still found the bass response to be very present and more than deep enough. And, it was coupled with a nice brightness that made percussion crisp and synths cutting. On a track like "Loyalty" by Kendrick Lamar, you'll find that the bass response is still plenty. The sub-bass content on this track takes the form of a bass line in the verse, and the headphones did a good job of producing it without overshadowing other aspects of the mix. Lamar and Rihanna's vocals were present and crisp, and the percussion had plenty of detail. There are some places in which you'll find that the detail isn't as impressive as what you'll get on newer headphones, like the XM6. On "Drover" by Bill Callahan, the details were plenty crisp, but there wasn't quite as much sizzle as you can find on newer, more expensive headphones, on instruments like the cymbals. Still, the rest of the track sounded superb—the driving kick drum had plenty of oomph, and Callahan's vocal was deep and vibrant. For orchestral music, like The Gospel According to the Other Mary by John Adams, I found the headphones deliver a wide, expansive soundstage that gave sections plenty of room to breathe without stepping on each other's toes. The vocal soloist also stood out, which made a difference. Microphone quality isn't bad, but newer headphones offer much better mic performance. In a recording, my voice sounded fine, and I could easily hear each word I said. But my voice didn't have much depth, and background noise leaked through much more than on newer headphones with newer suppression tech. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Sony WH-1000XM4C headphones keep everything that made the original XM4 excellent. They have that beloved design, with newer connectivity tech and an upgraded app, plus they sound superb and offer the best ANC you can get at this price point. If you're looking for a great pair of do-it-all headphones at $300 or so, these are an easy recommendation. They're cheaper than the Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) and offer much of what Bose does at that lower price. If you are willing to spend a little more, you’ll get better ANC from Bose, along with USB-C audio support, though you’ll trade away some of the customization options the Sony headphones offer through their app, like more advanced EQ. The XM4C headphones are also quite a bit better than the Fender Mix, with better sound and ANC, although Fender wins comfortably on battery life. Christian de Looper is a freelance consumer tech reporter based in sunny Santa Cruz, California. With a Bachelor's Degree in Music Technology, Christian leverages his industry knowledge to review audio products for PCMag, including Bluetooth headphones and speakers. He also contributes to Tom’s Guide, Digital Trends, Mashable, ZDNet, and others, where he reviews audio, mobile, smart home, and computing gear.

item.title: REVIEW: JSAUX FlipGo dual-screen portable monitor review: Gorgeous displays with touch support and a built-in USB hub
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
The JSAUX FlipGo is an impeccable dual-screen portable monitor, although it’s more suited for your desk than a laptop bag. - +Incredible build quality in this class - +Built-in hub gives you two USB-A ports and a USB-C port - -4.2-pound weight pushes the limit for a “portable” monitor Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. The FlipGo is yet another entry into the portable dual-monitor field from JSAUX (the previous one being the more ambitious FlipGo Horizon Pro), and it definitely makes a good first impression. Not only do you get two 16-inch 2560 x 1600 IPS displays, but the FlipGo also supports touch input (on Windows systems). In addition, it incorporates a built-in USB hub that gives you two additional USB-A ports and one USB-C port for your peripherals. JSAUX provides all of this functionality in a product that comes in at a bit under $500, which is in line with other portable dual-monitors on the market. However, there’s a hefty toll for the functionality that’s provided in this package for those expecting to actually use it as a travel companion. Design of the JSAUX FlipGo (PM0204) When I first received the shipping box for the FlipGo, I was shocked at how large and heavy it was. My shock was made even more apparent when I removed the FlipGo from its protective padding, revealing a massive dual-screen device weighing an incredible 4.18 pounds. That’s more than half a pound heavier than a 14-inch Apple MacBook Pro. The choice of materials contributes to the 4+ pound weight of the FlipGo. JSAUX uses a thick aluminum chassis that resists flexing and feels incredibly premium to the touch. That premium feel even extends to the hinges that connect the two displays. They are robust, with no play, allowing you to easily open the FlipGo to whatever display angle you desire. While JSAUX labels the FlipGo as a “portable” monitor, this is not something that you’ll be able to easily slip into a laptop bag or even a backpack. The dual 16-inch screen frame measures 14.41 x 9.45 inches and is 0.7 inches thick. For most people, the FlipGo will take up a permanent residence on your desk, or perhaps travel with you from one side of your office building to the other. But carrying it around for travel seems like a bridge too far. With that said, the specs on the FlipGo are quite impressive. You get two 16-inch 60 Hz IPS displays, each with a resolution of 2560 x 1600. Considering that most competitors in this space give you dual 1920 x 1080 panels, this resolution upgrade is much appreciated here. Both screens feature a glossy finish, which is uncommon for dual-screen monitors. However, that’s because both panels support 10-point touch input natively in Windows 11. Unfortunately, touch input is not supported in macOS, so you’ll want to consider the FlipGo (non-touch) if you’re a Mac user. Connectivity-wise, the FlipGo’s primary ports are on the left side of the bottom panel. Here you’ll find two USB-C ports and two mini-HDMI ports. On the right side of the bottom panel, you’ll find ports provided by the internal USB hub: two USB-A and one USB-C. Adjacent to the USB hub hookups is a three-way jog wheel for the OSD and the power button. JSAUX offers a stand that allows you to prop the FlipGo up in landscape (one monitor stacked on top of the other) or portrait mode (both monitors standing up vertically, book-style). However, our review unit only came with a red faux leather protective cover. Without the stand, I could use the monitor with the bottom panel sitting flat on my desk and the top panel sitting vertically. Alternatively, I could use it in portrait mode. OSD on the JSAUX FlipGo (PM0204) The FlipGo uses a relatively basic on-screen display (OSD), which is controlled using a three-way jog wheel. Despite there being two displays, you don’t have independent control over picture settings. Adjustments made on one display apply to both, for better or worse. You can flick the wheel right or left to adjust brightness up or down. Moving up and down with the jog wheel navigates through the OSD, while pressing on it takes you one level deeper until you select an option (similar to the previously reviewed FlipGo Horizon Pro). Likewise, pressing once on the power button takes you back one menu, and a long press turns off the monitor. You’ll find the usual assortment of adjustable settings in the OSD, like brightness, contrast, and sharpness. There’s a separate menu for color temperature, saturation, and hue. There are also options to switch between HDMI and USB-C inputs. Connecting and Operating the JSAUX FlipGo (PM0204) The FlipGo comes with an assortment of cables in the box. You get two USB-C cables, a mini-HDMI to HDMI cable, and a USB-C wall adapter. As I previously mentioned, the FlipGo does not support touch input on macOS. In addition, the FlipGo only supports mirror mode for both screens on macOS and requires you to use both USB-C and mini-HDMI to HDMI cables to connect (Windows 11 supports both mirror and extend modes). Because of these limitations and the fact that you’d be better off buying the cheaper non-touch model for macOS, I performed all of my testing with a Windows 11 laptop (HP OminiBook X). Setting up the FlipGo couldn’t have been easier. Although JSAUX includes two mini-HDMI ports on the FlipGo for use with older laptops, if you have a USB-C port that supports DisplayPort, you can use that instead. With my OmniBook X test laptop, I was able to use just one USB-C cable to handle both power and video/data for the FlipGo. The FlipGo also supports 60-watt power passthrough to your laptop, which you can leverage by running dedicated power through the second USB-C port. Using just a single cable between the FlipGo and the OmniBook X, I primarily used the two displays in portrait mode. In this mode, I could have two separate webpages open, side-by-side next to the OmniBook X’s internal panel. While I could use the FlipGo in landscape mode, the bottom panel had to lie flat on my desk, given that no stand was provided with my review unit to prop it up. Touch support functioned, as expected, on both panels without needing to install any additional software. In short, the FlipGo operated flawlessly. Display Performance on the JSAUX FlipGo (PM0204) The FlipGo uses two 16-inch IPS panels, each with a resolution of 2560 x 1600 and a refresh rate of 60 Hz. JSAUX listed maximum brightness at 500 nits, but as you’ll see with our test numbers below, that figure was quite optimistic. As I previously stated, due to the lack of a stand provided with my review unit, I primarily used the FlipGo in portrait mode, and it performed wonderfully here. The large panel sizes combined with the extra resolution over 1080p panels made them ideal for putting two webpages side-by-side. More frequently, I found myself pairing a webpage with an instance of Microsoft Word or Microsoft Excel. I especially appreciated the extra vertical resolution to limit scrolling up and down in Excel. Compared to the FlipGo Horizon Pro that I previously reviewed, the panels on the “regular” FlipGo were far superior. Not only were they much more colorful and vibrant, but they were also vastly superior in brightness (319 nits versus 247.4 nits). However, I must note that the 319 nits that we recorded were a far cry from the 500 nits that JSAUX claims. For our color tests, the FlipGo covered 97.2 percent of DCI-P3 and 137.2 percent of sRGB color spaces. That put the FlipGo well ahead of its competition, with the Aura Triple Aero 15.6 Pro Max coming the closest (at 85.4 percent and 120.6 percent, respectively). Given the higher-quality panels on the FlipGo compared to the FlipGo Horizon Pro and the glossy finish on my OmniBook X’s display, overall color balance matched pretty well across all three displays, adding to the enjoyment of using the portable monitor. I’ve often found that portable monitors have slightly (and sometimes far) inferior panels than their laptop counterparts, which can lead to a jarring experience when looking from one to the other. That is definitely not the case with the FlipGo. The JSAUX FlipGo is a remarkable piece of hardware for productivity warriors. At first sight, the FlipGo impresses with its high-quality build, stiff hinges, and plentiful video input options. JSAUX even incorporates a USB hub that gives you a couple of USB-A ports and a USB-C port to expand your peripheral footprint. The FlipGo also tops the charts when it comes to color performance and brightness, more than justifying its $479 street price. I have two reservations concerning my review unit, but only one is really applicable. My review unit lacked a stand to prop the FlipGo up in landscape or portrait modes; however, shipping units from Amazon now include that part. So, crisis averted on that front. My other complaint is unavoidable: the 4.18-pound weight is considerable and is probably a bit more than most people are willing to deal with when traveling. However, it makes a perfect companion for expanding real estate on your desk without the massive footprint that comes with hooking up a traditional desktop monitor.

item.title: REVIEW: De'Longhi Magnifica Start review: good coffee, confusing controls
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
The De'Longhi Magnifica Start is an appealing entry-level automatic coffee machine if you’re going to be satisfied with a limited selection of drinks. It produces consistently good espresso with an appealing crema, while the LatteCrema automatic milk-frothing system delivers impressive results with both dairy and plant-based milk. Its compact dimensions are another advantage, particularly for smaller kitchens, although I found the controls and customization options took some getting used to. Despite needing a little patience initially, I found that the Magnifica Start offers plenty of functionality for its price and the results make the effort worthwhile. - +LatteCrema system works with a variety of milk types Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. De'Longhi Magnifica Start: Two-minute review The De'Longhi Magnifica Start is one of the Italian manufacturer's more affordable automatic bean-to-cup coffee machines, designed to take much of the effort out of preparing fresh coffee at home. It doesn't offer the extensive drinks menu or customization options of more expensive models, but it benefits from the company's LatteCrema automatic milk frothing system, making it a potentially appealing choice for anyone who enjoys milk-based coffee. The particular model I have on test here, the ECAM220.61.W, offers just four one-touch functions — namely espresso, coffee, latte macchiato and hot water — meaning only three are actually coffee drinks. Other versions of the Magnifica Start offer different selections, so it's worth double-checking exactly which model you're buying. Despite its relatively basic specification, this Magnifica Start is a good-looking machine, with a smart white finish and a minimalist control panel. It certainly looks like it should be straightforward to operate but, as I discovered, it takes a little time to master. The controls aren't quite as intuitive as those on some other machines I've tested, such as the KitchenAid KF2, which offers similar functionality but has clearly labelled buttons that make preparing coffee incredibly straightforward. The Magnifica Start's steeper learning curve isn't necessarily a deal breaker, but it's something to be aware of. There are plenty of positives, though. Espresso shots are consistently well extracted with an appealing layer of crema, and I was impressed by how quickly the machine could prepare them, taking just 30 seconds from pressing the button to the finished drink. I did, however, find that adjusting the grinder to a slightly coarser setting produced a noticeably more satisfying flavor. The LatteCrema system also impressed me, producing a generous amount of foam with a pleasing texture using oat milk. While I still prefer the finer control offered by a traditional steam wand, it's still a capable alternative for anyone who wants the convenience of automatic milk frothing. The clearly marked milk carafe also takes thesome guesswork out of preparing drinks, while dishwasher-safe components help make cleaning easier. Honestly, for just a one- or two-person household, it’s easy to recommend the De'Longhi Magnifica Start, especially since its compact design makes it a good option for smaller kitchens, too. It may require a little patience initially, as the brewing adjustments aren’t as intuitive as I would have liked, but the results are worth spending that little extra time at the start to familiarize yourself with the instructions. De'Longhi Magnifica Start review: Price and availability - Different variants of the Magnifica Start are available in different markets - Model on test available in the UK and Australia; US version comes with an additional preset - List price: $749.95 / £399.99 / AU$799 The Magnifica Start is the entry-level machine within De’Longhi’s wider selection of automatic coffee makers. Within it, however, there are multiple variants that may look virtually identical, yet offer different features, so it's important to pay attention to the model number. For example, the exact model number of my review unit is ECAM220.61.W, which is only available in Australia for AU$799, exclusively through De'Longhi's online store. A black variant, with model number ECAM220.63.B, is available at a wider selection of third-party retailers, although it replaces the ‘latte macchiato’ preset on my review model with ‘cappuccino mix’. There’s yet another model that replaces the LatteCrema system with a manual steam wand. While this particular white model is specific to Australia, similar versions are available internationally. In the US, for example, the comparable ECAM22080B retails for $749.95, but benefits from an additional cappuccino preset, bringing its total number of one-touch functions to five. In the UK meanwhile, the ECAM220.61.GB is a closely related model finished in dark grey. It offers the same four one-touch functions as the model reviewed and carries a £399.99 recommended retail price. Given its limited selection of drinks, the Magnifica Start can be compared with the KitchenAid KF2 released earlier in 2026. It, too, has a relatively small selection of presets, although it uses a Pannarello steam wand for milk frothing as opposed to the automatic LatteCrema system on the De'Longhi. The KF2 also adds iced coffee to the mix, although I found the results to be something of a mixed bag. On price alone, the Magnifica Start is the clear winner of the two. However, I have to mention the Ninja Luxe Café as a viable alternative. It retails for $599.99 / £579.99 / AU$849 (or less as it’s often discounted), and while it might be a more hands-on machine, it offers considerably greater versatility than the De’Longhi, including the ability to prepare cold brew and filter coffee. There's also the option of moving up, both in price and size, to the De'Longhi Magnifica Evo Next, which retails for $1,099.95 / £649.96 / AU$1,149. It uses a similar brewing system to the Magnifica Start, but offers a more comprehensive selection of drink presets and a colour display for easier navigation. De'Longhi Magnifica Start review: Design - Attractive, compact design with a minimalist control panel - Only three coffee presets on model reviewed, with no dedicated cappuccino or hot-milk function - Clearly marked milk carafe and dishwasher-safe components No matter which model of the De'Longhi Magnifica Start is available in your location, they’re all identical. The only real differences are whether it uses the LatteCrema system or a steam wand, the color of the machine and the number of drink recipes it offers. It’s an attractive coffee machine, particularly in the glossy white finish of the model sent for this review. The Magnifica Start has a relatively minimalist appearance, with a predominantly plastic construction and a black control panel providing some contrast. I’d argue it doesn't have quite the same premium appeal as the KitchenAid KF2 and KitchenAid KF3 I've reviewed previously, but I think it looks smart enough for most kitchens. It measures 24 x 44 x 35cm (W x D x H), making it a relatively compact appliance for a fully automatic coffee machine. That said, its 24cm width might be a small footprint, but its 44cm depth is worth considering if you have a particularly narrow countertop. The machine's compact dimensions should also make it a reasonable option for kitchens with low-hanging cabinets. You will, of course, need some clearance above it to remove the lid and refill the hopper, but I didn't find accessing it to be particularly troublesome. The bean hopper, located on top of the machine towards the rear, can accommodate up to 250g of beans and is covered by a lid that unfortunately doesn't form a completely airtight seal, meaning the beans will lose freshness if left in the hopper for more than a couple of days. The Magnifica Start also accepts pre-ground coffee via a separate chute on top of the machine, and a measuring scoop is included in the box. While I'd generally recommend using freshly ground beans wherever possible, it's a useful addition if you occasionally fancy a decaf but don't want to empty the hopper of your regular beans. Another design feature I appreciate is the positioning of the water reservoir, which slides out from the front-right side of the machine. I praised this same arrangement in my De’Longhi Magnifica Evo Next review, and I'm pleased to see it make an appearance on a more entry-level model. It makes refilling the tank incredibly easy, particularly compared with machines that have their reservoirs located at the rear — like those from KitchenAid — and might require you to move the entire machine to gain access. The reservoir also looks deceptively small, but holds a generous 1.8L of water, matching the capacity of the more expensive Magnifica Evo Next. The drip tray covers the entire depth of the machine and slides out from the front, along with the internal container that collects used coffee grounds. The latter can hold up to 14 coffee pucks before needing to be emptied — far more generous than the KitchenAid KF4 that I use at home, which can only hold six or seven used pucks before it needs emptying. On the front, you'll find the removable LatteCrema milk carafe, which attaches alongside the height-adjustable coffee dispensing spouts. It slots into place easily and takes care of milk frothing automatically, removing the need for a separate steam wand. The carafe can be swapped out for a water spout if you wish to pour hot water for a tea instead. The particular model under test here features De'Longhi's LatteCrema Hot system, although more expensive models, such as the Eletta Explore, can also come with a separate LatteCrema Cool carafe for preparing cold milk foam. Its absence here isn't especially surprising given the Magnifica Start's more affordable positioning. One feature I particularly appreciate here is the measurement markings on the carafe to indicate how much milk you should add for your chosen drink. This helps minimize waste, especially if you're only making coffee for one person. Interestingly, there are markings for ‘cappuccino’ and ‘cappuccino mix’ coffees, neither of which is available as a preset on this particular Magnifica Start, but is a present for the model sold in the US. The carafe also has an automatic cleaning function, while several removable components, including the drip tray and milk carafe, are dishwasher-safe. The control panel is similarly minimalist, with four prominent drink icons and separate buttons for adjusting coffee strength and accessing other settings and functions, such as cleaning modes. On the surface, it looks incredibly straightforward, which is exactly what I'd expect from a machine offering such a limited selection of drinks. However, I didn't find it quite as intuitive as I'd hoped. The layout initially led me to believe I should select my desired drink before adjusting its strength, whereas the machine actually requires you to select the strength first. It's something that becomes easier with familiarity, but I do think the controls could have been better explained. The Magnifica Start lacks dedicated user profiles, something that I’ve come to appreciate on other automatic espresso machines I’ve reviewed. While you can customize individual drink quantities and adjust coffee strength, there’s only one saved volume setting per recipe. This means that if two people prefer different-sized coffees, they’ll have to keep adjusting the programmed volumes to suit their tastes. Combined with its limited selection of drinks, I think this makes the Magnifica Start best suited to a single person or couple, particularly if both enjoy similar coffees. Larger households with different preferences would likely benefit from a machine with user profiles and a more extensive drink menu. De'Longhi Magnifica Start review: Performance - Consistent espresso extraction with a good layer of crema - LatteCrema produces impressive milk texture, although a manual steam wand offers greater control - Quick coffee preparation, but some functions take time to master As with any bean-to-cup coffee machine, the most important consideration is how well the De'Longhi Magnifica Start actually makes the drink. Ease of use is a close second, especially for a machine designed to simplify the process of preparing your favourite drinks at home. My first experience with the Magnifica Start was something of a mixed bag. Setting it up was relatively straightforward, but I soon discovered that getting it to produce the exact drink I wanted would require some experimentation. My first latte macchiato, for example, dispensed considerably more liquid than I had anticipated, almost causing my cup to overflow. Part of the problem is that there's no clear indication of precisely how much coffee or milk each preset will dispense, at least not without referring to the full user manual on De'Longhi's website. While coffee strength can be adjusted before preparing each drink, there's only one saved volume setting per recipe. To adjust the volume of any drink, press and hold its dedicated button for a few seconds until the light blinks rapidly. The built-in grinder will have already kicked into action, which is normal. Once the coffee (or milk if you’re customizing the latte macchiato) reaches your desired level, press the same drink button again and the settings will be saved. Once I'd figured out the process, I was able to customize the volume of my latte macchiato successfully, and the Magnifica Start remembered my settings for subsequent drinks. However, restoring the original quantity isn't quite as convenient. While it's possible to reset drink volumes to their factory defaults, doing so also resets all other settings and customized recipes. This seems unnecessarily cumbersome if you simply want to undo a change to one drink. While I appreciate that all automatic coffee machines require some familiarization, I found myself returning to the user manual more often than I'd expected from a machine with such a limited selection of drinks. There's also an amusing inconsistency in the setup guidance, which recommends preparing several cappuccinos before expecting the machine to deliver its best results. That's perfectly reasonable advice for a machine with a cappuccino preset, but this particular version of the Magnifica Start doesn't have one. It's a minor detail, admittedly, but it adds to the impression that the instructions aren't tailored as carefully as they could be to the individual machine. Fortunately, when it comes to actually making coffee, the Magnifica Start has proved to be a reliable performer. After preparing several espressos, I found extraction quality to be consistently good, with each shot producing an appealing layer of golden-caramel crema. The results were remarkably similar from one coffee to the next, suggesting the machine has little trouble delivering a repeatable extraction. I wasn't initially sold on the flavor, however, particularly as I've used the same beans in other machines, including KitchenAid's semi-automatic and fully automatic models, with more satisfying results. Fortunately, adjusting the grinder to produce a slightly coarser grind had a noticeably positive effect, resulting in a more enjoyable espresso. It goes to show that while the Magnifica Start is capable of producing good coffee, some experimentation may be required to get the best results. The De’Longhi Magnifica Start doesn’t feature any kind of intelligent grind adjustment — De’Longhi does have its own BeanAdapt technology to do just that, but it’s reserved for its higher-end models — so you’ll need to adjust the grind yourself if you’re not totally satisfied with the results. By default, the grinder is set to position four of seven, which De’Longhi claims “has been factory set to ensure that coffee is prepared correctly”. If coffee is being dispensed particularly slowly, the grind may be too fine, in which case De'Longhi recommends adjusting the dial towards a higher number. You’ll need to turn the grind dial, found inside the bean hopper, towards a higher number. Conversely, if you want a fuller bodied or creamier coffee, then you’ll need to turn the dial towards position one. In either case, the grind dial should only be adjusted when the grinder is in motion, and it takes at least two poured coffees for results to take effect. I was pleased with the temperature of the finished coffee, which I found to be comfortably hot without being unpleasant to drink. If you prefer your coffee a little hotter or cooler, the brewing temperature can be adjusted through the machine's settings. What surprised me most, however, was just how quickly the Magnifica Start could prepare an espresso. I timed it at just 30 seconds from pressing the espresso button to the finished drink, which is impressively brisk for a machine that grinds fresh beans for each cup. It's also relatively quiet in operation. I recorded an average noise level of approximately 69dB using decibelX app in my iPhone in a quiet room and standing right in front of the machine, rising to around 74dB during grinding before dropping to 65dB while brewing. While the grinder is clearly audible, I never found the noise particularly intrusive, especially given how quickly the machine completes the process. Milk-based drinks take a little longer to brew, as the LatteCrema system needs time to heat up before it can start dispensing milk. Even so, the overall process remains convenient, particularly as there's no need to manually froth milk or transfer it between containers. Speaking of which, I was pleasantly surprised by the performance of the LatteCrema milk frothing system. I've used it on other De'Longhi coffee machines in the past and haven't always been completely convinced by its ability to produce the milk texture I prefer, particularly when using plant-based alternatives. This time, however, the results have been noticeably better. Using oat milk, the Magnifica Start produced a generous amount of foam with a satisfyingly smooth texture, making for a more convincing latte macchiato than I had anticipated. I achieved similar results with dairy milk too. That being said, it's worth mentioning that the type of milk used can have a significant impact on frothing performance. If you’re using non-dairy varieties, it’s always recommended to use barista-style versions, as these are generally formulated to produce a more stable foam. I still prefer the results I can achieve with a traditional steam wand and, while I haven't had the chance to use it myself, a version of the De’Longhi Magnifica Start is available with one. A manual wand gives me far greater control over how much air I introduce into the milk, allowing me to create the finer, silkier microfoam I typically prefer for a flat white. But manual frothing also requires more skill and effort, and that's where the LatteCrema system makes a strong case for itself. For anyone who values convenience over having complete control of their milk texture, it's a capable set-and-forget solution that produces pleasing results with minimal input. Should you buy the De'Longhi Magnifica Start? Buy it if... You want a straightforward selection of coffee drinks If you primarily drink espresso, black coffee or latte macchiato, the Magnifica Start offers those essentials without overwhelming you with dozens of options. The LatteCrema system takes care of frothing milk for you, and its removable carafe has measurements to help minimize waste. You want a coffee machine that's easy to clean An automatic milk-system cleaning function and dishwasher-safe components should make routine maintenance easier. Don't buy it if... You enjoy a wide variety of coffee drinks With no dedicated cappuccino, flat white or standalone hot-milk function, this particular Magnifica Start is one of the more limited automatic machines I've tested. You expect completely intuitive controls The buttons look simple enough, but understanding how to adjust drink strength and serving sizes requires a little patience. While you can adjust coffee strength and drink length, you don't get the extensive personalization available on more expensive automatic coffee machines. De'Longhi Magnifica Start review: Also consider The KF2 is just as compact as the De'Longhi, and also has a limited selection of drinks, but I found it easier to use. The steam wand is more reliable for producing thick, velvety foam too. This 3-in-1 machine from Ninja can do espresso, cold brew and drip coffee, all for a similar price as the De'Longhi. It does require more manual input than the fully automatic Magnifica Start, but it's near-foolproof control system will have you experimenting with your morning brew in no time. How I tested the De'Longhi Magnifica Start I tested the De'Longhi Magnifica Start in the TechRadar Australia office kitchen, using it to prepare coffee with Campos Superior beans, a medium-dark blend that’s roasted locally in Sydney, Australia, where I’m based. I prepared multiple espresso and milk-based drinks to assess extraction consistency, flavour and milk texture, using both dairy milk and barista-style oat milk. I also experimented with the grinder settings to determine their effect on espresso flavour. I evaluated how straightforward the machine was to set up and use, paying particular attention to its control panel and customization options. I used a measuring cup to check that customized drink volumes were remembered correctly, and recorded the time taken to prepare an espresso, along with noise levels during grinding and brewing.
