item.title: REVIEW: HUAWEI Watch GT 7 Pro review: I took a chance on the loud one, and it wowed me in unexpected ways
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
“Built for adventure. Born to stand out.”
- Premium titanium, ceramic, and sapphire construction - Bright, sunlight-readable AMOLED display - Reliable GPS and useful trail navigation - Excellent fitness tracking and battery endurance - No eSIM or standalone cellular connectivity The HUAWEI Watch GT 7 Pro gets the things I care about right: dependable GPS on hikes, a bright outdoor display, useful cardio tracking, a tough build, and battery life that lets me forget where I put the charger. I was skeptical of the green finish at first, but two months later, I’m converted. I’ve knocked it against things, taken it on trips and treks, and worn it without a screen protector. It still looks pristine. More importantly, its walk-back navigation has proved genuinely useful outdoors, and I regularly get more than ten days of battery life. It’s not perfect, of course. App support is more limited than on Wear OS or watchOS, iPhone notifications have a few frustrating blind spots, there’s no eSIM, and Curve Pay depends on regional support. I also caught the watch awarding me phantom steps while driving. Its larger case isn’t particularly inviting at bedtime, either, although that’s as much about my dislike of sleeping with a watch as it is about the hardware. These are real compromises, but they don’t undo what the GT 7 Pro does well. My take is fairly straightforward on this one. Buy it for battery life, outdoor tracking, durability, and a sporty premium design. Think twice if a huge app ecosystem, standalone cellular connectivity, or consistent overnight tracking matters more than going days without charging. Note: I tested the European version while living in India and traveling in the US. Prices, warranty coverage, and supported services vary by region, so check local availability before importing. HUAWEI Watch GT 7 Pro design and durability: The green one got me I have a type. Give me a silver case, a black strap, perhaps a nice brown leather band, and I’m already nodding approvingly like a man who has just discovered a tasteful chair. Loud watch colors have never been my natural habitat. So when I first saw the green GT 7 Pro, my reaction was that it’s something I’d absolutely not buy. Then I wore it. Annoyingly, Huawei was right. The green finish has grown on me considerably. It’s sporty and distinctive without looking like a neon running vest escaped onto my wrist. It loosely reminds me of some green Swatch or Seiko designs, although that’s an aesthetic comparison, not a claim about watchmaking. The GT 7 Pro has its own personality, and I like that it doesn’t look like every other black-and-silver smartwatch. The GT line has also taken a more athletic turn. Earlier generations struck me as a little more office-friendly; this one looks ready to clock out and go cycling. If the goal is a watch that disappears beneath a shirt cuff, the angular bezel and color-matched strap might be too much. I expected to miss the more classic look. Thankfully, over time I’ve realized that I don’t. Huawei has also picked reassuring materials: a titanium alloy case, a nano-tech ceramic bezel, and sapphire glass over the display. Those specifications sound good on paper, but my more meaningful test was my own clumsiness. I’ve knocked the watch against objects, had a few mishaps, and taken it on trips and treks. After around two months, it remains pristine, with no screen scratches despite going without a protector and no visible scuffs on the metal edges. Of course, this isn’t a laboratory durability test, and I wouldn’t recommend launching a smartwatch at a doorframe to see what happens. My point is that I simply haven’t babied the GT 7 Pro, and it has held up beautifully. And if you’re just as rough a user (read: clumsy) as me, that might matter more than another animated watch face. The strap deserves a mention, too. Its design tucks the end underneath for a neat finish, and a quick-release button makes swapping Huawei’s own straps easy. Standard 22 mm quick-release third-party bands fit as well, which gives buyers plenty of room to personalize the watch. There is a small catch: some Huawei bands use a proprietary metal piece or guide rail to create a seamless finish. A generic band might leave a small gap or lack the anti-pivoting extension. In other words, fits and looks like it came from the factory aren’t always the same promise. HUAWEI Watch GT 7 Pro display: A screen that handles the actual sun I’ve worn the GT 7 Pro outdoors on trips, hikes, and treks, including in direct sunlight. The screen has remained easy to read. I haven’t had to perform that familiar smartwatch ritual of cupping my wrist like I’m whispering a secret to the display. The 1.47-inch AMOLED panel has a resolution of 466 x 466 pixels, with Huawei claiming peak brightness of up to 3,000 nits. It’s worth noting that figure is a laboratory maximum under a particular test condition, not an all-day brightness setting. However, what matters to me is the real-world result: I could check the time, workout data, and navigation information outside without constantly searching for shade. The only caveat is the size. Huawei offers the GT 7 Pro in one 46 mm size, and the watch has a noticeable presence on the wrist. At around 55.5 grams without the strap, it feels like a substantial piece of hardware. I enjoy that during the day; at bedtime, even a little wrist hardware isn’t my idea of luxury. HUAWEI Watch GT 7 Pro fitness tracking: My gym watch has hiking ambitions Huawei gives the GT 7 Pro a big outdoor-sports identity, with support for activities including skiing, cycling, and golf, alongside more than 100 workout modes and route-guidance features. I cycled with it during my initial testing, but over the longer term, I spent more time at the gym and out hiking. That’s where my firsthand experience is strongest. At the gym, the watch doesn’t magically identify every exercise or count every set for me. It may recognize that I’ve been active and report a 25- or 30-minute workout, but it won’t reliably know whether I was doing squats or negotiating with a cable machine. I don’t consider that a major flaw; distinguishing individual movements requires context, and a watch isn’t going to read my mind just because I strapped it on. I tried generic free-training logging, but didn’t find it particularly useful. Cardio is a better fit. On the treadmill, cross trainer, and rowing machine, I found the tracking useful and accurate in everyday use. I start the session, get on with the workout, and review the data afterward. The results have felt coherent rather than decorative. That’s my experience, not the result of a controlled comparison against specialist equipment. The GT 7 Pro also tracks heart rate, blood oxygen, sleep, and stress-related measures, with ECG and pulse-wave analysis features available where supported. Its Physical Readiness feature combines signals such as sleep, recent activity, heart-rate variability (HRV), and stress into a daily recovery-style guide. I like having that context, provided it’s treated as guidance rather than gospel. Because, let’s be real, a wrist notification isn’t qualified to diagnose me after one restless Tuesday. My small fitness gremlin is the step counter. I sometimes notice around 100–200 extra steps, often while driving. Movement from steering can fool wrist-based counters, and this isn’t a Huawei-exclusive problem. Still, a little more contextual logic could help. The GT 7 Pro occasionally gives my driving a modest walking bonus. Generous, perhaps, but not especially useful. HUAWEI Watch GT 7 Pro GPS and hiking: The feature I reached for most GPS has been a genuine strength for me. I came from the Amazfit GTR 4, and Huawei’s positioning has been excellent by comparison in my experience. I used the GT 7 Pro on hikes in the US, remote treks, and in more remote parts of Hawaii. I didn’t conduct a satellite bake-off, but I also didn’t encounter practical tracking problems that undermined those trips. My favorite feature was walk-back navigation. I had Google Maps downloaded on my phone as a backup while the watch recorded the trek. When it was time to head back toward my starting point, I enjoyed using the watch’s return guidance instead of immediately pulling out my phone. It was easy to check, a little interactive, and genuinely handy. That’s the sort of feature that earns space on my wrist. It helped in an actual situation rather than simply adding another tile to a menu that looks impressive in screenshots. Huawei uses dual-band, multi-system satellite positioning and newer algorithms intended to estimate movement when satellite reception drops. Naturally, GPS performance can vary with terrain, tree cover, buildings, and settings. Someone running through a dense urban environment might have a different experience from mine on open hiking routes. Thankfully, in my testing, routes went well, and the watch gave me confidence outdoors. HUAWEI Watch GT 7 Pro battery life: My favorite personality trait Considering the fact that I use an iPhone as my daily driver, the one question I often get asked is why I don’t use an Apple Watch, and the answer to that is basically this: I don’t want another device demanding a daily charging appointment. I already travel with enough cables to open a small electronics shop. Thankfully, the GT 7 Pro doesn’t ask to join the queue every night. I regularly get more than ten days of battery life, and sometimes close to two weeks. There’s an important caveat: I don’t routinely sleep in the watch, so my personal results don’t include consistent overnight tracking. Huawei rates the GT 7 Pro for up to 21 days with light use, 12 days under typical use, seven days with the always-on display enabled, and up to 51 hours in trail-running mode. Those are manufacturer estimates, not promises that every user will see the same results. GPS workouts, screen settings, calls, and health monitoring all affect runtime. Still, my experience has been excellent, and I haven’t needed to micromanage the battery. The real benefit is the absence of battery anxiety. I can travel without packing yet another charger for nightly use, and I don’t keep checking whether the watch will die before I do. It becomes something I use rather than another gadget I have to maintain. Charging is wireless and fast enough that I haven’t felt inconvenienced. Would USB-C be tidier? Absolutely. One less proprietary accessory in my travel bag would be lovely. But I’ll take this endurance over a more satisfying cable arrangement. HUAWEI Watch GT 7 Pro sleep tracking: Good when I use it, which isn’t often As I said, I tested sleep tracking a handful of times. The GT 7 Pro recognized daytime naps, and its REM and deep-sleep estimates looked reasonable alongside those from my Amazfit watch. I didn’t see an obvious reason to distrust the results from those limited sessions. But here’s the thing: I don’t like sleeping in watches. This isn’t a GT 7 Pro complaint so much as a “my wrist wants to be left alone while I’m unconscious” complaint. Even a small amount of weight can distract me when I’m trying to get comfortable. I’ve worn heavier Garmin watches, so the Huawei isn’t unusually heavy; it’s just that my tolerance for wrist hardware in bed is simply low. The watch performed well in the sessions I tried, but I didn’t wear it every night for a long-term comparison. That’s an important distinction, and I’m not going to pretend otherwise just to make the review sound more comprehensive. If overnight tracking is a priority, comfort matters just as much as the data. A smart ring might suit people who want sleep insights without wearing a watch to bed, although it won’t replace the GT 7 Pro’s display, GPS, or workout interface. HUAWEI Watch GT 7 Pro software and connectivity: The app is good now, with a little bummer I received the GT 7 Pro before launch and initially used a beta version of Huawei Health. There were a couple of setup hiccups, with some sections purely in Chinese, but things settled down after I switched to the stable app when it became available. Watch faces are easy to browse and sync quickly, and Huawei Health has worked well for my regular use. That said, the GT 7 Pro isn’t running Wear OS or watchOS, and buyers shouldn’t expect the same app ecosystem. You get health and sports tools, Bluetooth calling, and the everyday basics, but not every phone app has a polished wrist-friendly counterpart. App availability and setup can also vary by phone and region, so Android users should check Huawei’s current installation instructions before buying. My most specific frustration came from using the watch with an iPhone. Emojis sometimes render incorrectly, WhatsApp images don’t appear in notifications, and quite surprisingly, Gmail isn’t listed among the notification options in Huawei Health. That last issue means I can’t enable Gmail alerts at all, so I’ve missed emails I would normally expect to see on my wrist. Most other notifications worked reliably, which makes the missing Gmail toggle particularly strange. This isn’t a claim that all iPhone notifications are broken; it’s one very important app-shaped hole in an otherwise functional experience. While we are on the topic of connectivity, it’s worth mentioning that there’s also no eSIM. That doesn’t bother me because I carry my phone anyway, but it matters if the idea is to leave the handset at home and still make calls or receive messages independently. Bluetooth calling and connected features rely on a nearby paired phone rather than standalone cellular connectivity, and thankfully the microphone is quite clear, and Bluetooth connectivity has been quite strong in my testing. NFC payments are another regional wrinkle. Huawei supports Curve Pay in eligible regions, but I couldn’t test it because I don’t have access to the service where I live. I can’t vouch for the payment experience. Having NFC hardware and having a supported payment service that works with a particular bank in a particular country are two very different things. Should you buy? The GT 7 Pro won me over where it matters to my routine. It survived my clumsy wrist, stayed readable in harsh sunlight, tracked cardio well, and gave me confidence on hikes. Walk-back navigation was genuinely useful, and the battery life is glorious: I regularly get more than ten days, sometimes close to two weeks, without needing to charge it every night. The step counter can over-credit my driving; I don’t wear the watch consistently for sleep tracking; and iPhone users should know about the emoji quirks, missing WhatsApp image previews, and absent Gmail notification option. There’s no eSIM, either, while Curve Pay depends on location. If a deep app ecosystem or phone-free connectivity is a priority, those are meaningful caveats rather than footnotes. A proper outdoor watch with everyday appeal But for a sturdy, premium-looking fitness watch with excellent endurance and dependable outdoor tracking, in my experience, I’m impressed. I started suspicious of the green finish and now think it looks great. I also spend a lot less time thinking about charging. That’s a pretty strong two-month performance from a gadget that’s supposed to make life easier, not give me another battery percentage to obsess over. The Galaxy Watch Ultra2 combines Wear OS app support with LTE connectivity, a display rated for up to 5,000 nits, and dedicated outdoor tools such as Trail Run. It’s the more compelling option for users who want a connected smartwatch that can also handle serious adventures. If an iPhone is the center of the universe, the Series 12 is the smartwatch that gets the assignment. Its tight Apple ecosystem integration, extensive health features, and broad app support make it a better fit for anyone who wants notifications, apps, and health data to work together seamlessly. Just be prepared for Apple’s claimed 24-hour battery life to make charging a much more regular part of the routine. The sensible sibling, the regular GT 7 offers much of the same fitness tracking, outdoor navigation, bright AMOLED display, and excellent battery life for less money. The main sacrifices are the Pro’s titanium construction, sapphire glass, ECG sensor, and diving features. Unless those extras matter, the standard GT 7 makes a strong case for keeping the change. I used the European version of the GT 7 Pro as my daily driver for around two months while living in India and traveling in the US. I wore it on hikes and remote treks, at the gym, and during treadmill, cross-trainer, and rowing workouts. I also tried cycling during my initial testing. I checked display visibility in direct sunlight, relied on GPS during hikes, and used walk-back guidance to return toward a trail starting point. My battery results came from normal use: usually more than ten days, sometimes close to two weeks. I don’t regularly wear the watch overnight, although I tested sleep tracking a handful of times, including daytime naps, and informally compared the results with my Amazfit. I used Huawei Health on an iPhone 16. FAQs (Frequently Asked Questions) Is the HUAWEI Watch GT 7 Pro good for hiking? Yes. GPS worked reliably for me on US hiking routes, remote treks, and in Hawaii. I also found the walk-back guidance genuinely useful when returning toward my starting point. GPS performance varies with terrain and conditions, so I’d still carry a phone and plan the route in advance. How long does the HUAWEI Watch GT 7 Pro battery last? Huawei rates it for up to 21 days with light use, 12 days under typical use, seven days with the always-on display, and up to 51 hours in trail-running mode. I regularly got more than ten days and sometimes close to two weeks, although I don’t routinely track sleep overnight. Settings, GPS workouts, and health monitoring will obviously affect battery life. Does the HUAWEI Watch GT 7 Pro work with an iPhone? Yes. It works with iPhones running iOS 13 or later through Huawei Health. Most third-party apps can have their notifications enabled as well, though your mileage may vary depending on the apps you use. Can I change the HUAWEI Watch GT 7 Pro’s strap? Yes. Huawei’s straps use a quick-release button, and standard 22 mm quick-release third-party bands fit. However, some generic straps may leave a small gap or lack the guide rail or anti-pivoting piece found on certain Huawei bands, so the fit and finish might not look quite as seamless. Can I make payments or use the HUAWEI Watch GT 7 Pro without my phone? The HUAWEI Watch GT 7 Pro supports NFC payments through Curve Pay in select regions, but it has no eSIM for standalone cellular connectivity. Bluetooth calling and other connected features require a nearby paired phone.

item.title: SALES: Best laptops for engineering students: Top 4 picks for power and portability
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
Engineering students are constantly on the move. Lectures, labs, libraries. That’s why you need a laptop that can handle your workload without making you feel like you’re lugging around a block of concrete. That’s why the laptops below strike such a good balance. They’re powerful for CAD and simulations, but they’re also light enough to throw in a bag and carry around campus. Why you should trust PCWorld for laptop reviews and buying advice: It’s in our name! PCWorld prides itself on laptop experience and expertise. We’ve been covering PCs since 1983, and we now review more than 70 laptops every year. All of the picks below have been personally tested and vetted by our experts, who’ve applied not only performance benchmarks but rigorous usability standards. We’re also committed to reviewing PC laptops at every price point to help you find a machine that matches your budget. - Good CPU and integrated GPU performance Who should buy the Asus Zenbook 14 OLED? The Asus Zenbook 14 OLED tops our list because of the brilliant combination of power, portability, and battery life. The AMD Ryzen 7 chip is designed to run heavier programs like CAD without slowing down, even if you’ve got a bunch of tabs open on the side. The 14-inch 1920×1200 OLED touchscreen also looks fantastic and will make your diagrams and other projects really pop. The one thing that really sticks out is the battery, though. Seriously, it went for over 16 hours in our test, which kind of blew my mind. You can definitely survive a whole day of classes, especially with conservative use and the brightness turned down. The audio is also quite good, offering you good volume and clarity during remote lectures. Asus Zenbook 14 OLED: Further considerations The build quality’s pretty good, especially considering it’s just $699 as of this writing. It’s also thin (0.59 inches) and light (2.82 pounds), which is great if you’re running from class to class. While the keyboard isn’t the best we’ve ever used because of the undersized keys, it’s totally fine for day-to-day use. Who should buy the Dell 14S? The Dell 14S is a great fit for engineering students who want a laptop that can easily last through a long day of classes. It actually delivered some of the longest runtimes we’ve seen (nearly 36 hours in our video playback test!), thanks in part to its efficient Intel Core Ultra 7 355 processor and 69 watt-hour battery. It’s also just a solid day-to-day machine. The aluminum design feels nice and sturdy, the keyboard is comfortable to type on for long periods of time, and the laptop remains easy to carry at just 3.28 pounds. For students who mainly use office apps, the Dell 14S has more than enough power for that kind of thing. This isn’t the laptop to buy if you need raw performance. The Dell 14S relies on Intel integrated graphics rather than a dedicated GPU, so it’s not the best choice for running demanding CAD projects. Ultimately, the Dell 14S is a portable, reliable machine for students who spend most of their day away from a desk. It puts efficiency first. Acer Nitro V 16 AI – Best for work and gaming on a budget - Large touchpad compared to alternatives - Good battery life for a budget gaming laptop - Terrible audio quality from built-in speakers - Wireless connectivity stuck on the Wi-Fi 6 standards - Slightly more expensive laptops offer better value Who should buy the Acer Nitro V 16 AI? If you’re an engineering student who likes to game after class, the Acer Nitro V 16 AI is worth considering. The RTX 5050 tucked inside delivers smooth 1080p gaming, hitting a respectable 72 FPS in Cyberpunk 2077 on Ultra settings. It also gives extra firepower for CAD modeling and rendering tasks. The 16-inch 1920×1200 IPS display is slightly taller than the typical 15.6-inch 1080p screens, so you’re getting more vertical workspace here–this is useful for coding, spreadsheets, and so on. At a price hovering between $800 and $900 it’s a budget-friendly option for students. Acer Nitro V 16 AI: Further considerations The AMD Ryzen 5 240 isn’t the fastest CPU around, and the speakers aren’t impressive, but despite these trade-offs, the Acer Nitro V 16 AI avoids common pitfalls most budget gaming laptops fall into. It lasted 12 hours on a single charge in testing, which is impressive for a gaming machine. The keyboard and touchpad are also spacious, making it comfortable to work on for long periods. Microsoft Surface Pro – Best ultraportable Who should buy the Microsoft Surface Pro? If you’re an engineering student with a jam-packed schedule, often needing to run from class to class, the Surface Pro is so lightweight (just a little over a pound) you’ll hardly notice its presence. Inside this laptop you’ll find a Snapdragon X Plus chip, so you can expect it to deliver a quiet, fanless experience (perfect for working in libraries and lecture halls), and it should handle basic coding and homework just fine. Note: Snapdragon X Plus / Arm models are fine for lighter coding and notes, but if your coursework is heavy on SolidWorks, Autodesk apps, or older MATLAB workflows an x86 Windows laptop is a safer bet for performance and app compatibility first. The 12-inch 2196×1464 screen offers sharp colors and touchscreen capabilities, allowing you to draw and take notes with the (optical) Slim Pen. Microsoft Surface Pro: Further considerations Though we really vibe with the high-resolution display, it’s a bit small if you’re the kind of person that has many windows open at once. Battery life is all over the place, ranging from two to three hours under heavy loads to 19 hours with light usage. You’re also limited to just two USB-C ports, so you’ll probably want to pick up a dock or hub. - Acer Swift Air 14: Acer’s Swift Air 14 mostly hits its mark as a solid budget productivity laptop. However, its 8GB of memory still can pose problems in certain scenarios. - Acer Aspire 16 AI: The Acer Aspire 16 AI isn’t perfect, but it’s lightweight, capable, and has such a beautiful OLED display that the reviewer kept reaching for it anyway. - Geekom GeekBook M16: The GeekBook M16 is a solid budget productivity laptop with outstanding battery life and build quality, but its weak display and limited graphics performance hold it back from being a true all-rounder. The PCWorld team puts each and every Windows laptop through a series of benchmarks that test GPU and CPU performance, battery life, and so on. The idea is to push the laptop to its limits and then compare it against others we’ve tested. Chromebooks, on the other hand, go through a series of web-based tests. For a much deeper look at our review methodology, check out how PCWorld tests laptops. Who curated this article? Hi, I’m Ashley Biancuzzo, and I oversee all laptop and Chromebook coverage at PCWorld. While you’ll see me review Chromebooks on occasion, I’m also really into the broader world of consumer tech. I spend a lot of time writing and thinking about where laptops are headed–from AI and sustainable designs to long-term trends. When I’m not deep in the world of tech, you’ll probably find me gaming, getting lost in a good book, or chilling with my rescue greyhound, Allen. How to choose the best laptop for engineering students The following are important questions to ask before making a purchase. How much power do you need? You’ll need a good amount of power. Engineering classes usually have you running some pretty heavy stuff like CAD, MATLAB, SolidWorks, and simulations. That stuff can slow your laptop down if it’s not up to the task, especially if you’ve got a bunch of apps open. A Core i5 or Ryzen 5 will get you through most of it, but if you want things to run smoother, a Core i7 or Ryzen 7 is where it’s at (so long as your wallet agrees). Is RAM important? For sure! You’ll be using code editors, compilers, simulation tools, sometimes all at once. RAM keeps your laptop from freezing up when you’ve got a ton going on. And with RAM prices being a bit volatile nowadays, it’s worth future-proofing if you can. 8GB might work if you’re just starting out, but 16GB is way better, especially later on when your classes get more intense. How much storage should you get? You’ll collect a ton of files–project folders, software installs, maybe some video editing or game dev work depending on your focus. We’d say go for at least 512GB SSD so you’re not constantly clearing space. If you can get 1TB, do it. It’s faster and gives you more breathing room for whatever your classes (or side hobbies) throw at you. What is the best laptop for engineering students? If you’re an engineering student who needs something light, fast, and reliable for coding or writing papers (plus a great screen and battery), the Asus Zenbook 14 OLED is a dang fine pick. What is the best budget laptop for engineering students? If you’re on a tight budget and just need a straightforward for lighter coding programs, the Acer Aspire Go 15 gets the job done for just under $500. Is battery life important for engineering students? Heck yeah! Long battery life means you can power through those long nights at the school library. What’s the ideal screen size for an engineering laptop? We’d say the best screen size is anywhere from 13- to 15-inches. It can’t be too cumbersome otherwise it’ll get difficult to carry around.

The team at PCWorld continually sorts through all of the daily computer sales and puts together a curated list of the best deals available. But not all deals are really deals, so we only choose those offered by reputable companies and that include great hardware to ensure you get the best value for your money. We’ve also included some helpful answers to common questions about buying a computer at the bottom of this article. If you’re considering a laptop instead, be sure to check out our best laptop deals. Which kind of desktop PC should you buy? For most people, a desktop tower offers the best balance of price, performance, and future upgrades. Mini PCs are better when space matters, while all-in-ones trade upgradeability for a cleaner and simpler setup. Gamers should prioritize a dedicated graphics card, while home and office users can usually save money with integrated graphics. Refurbished desktops can also be excellent value if they come from a reputable seller with a warranty. Our desktop computer deals are chosen by computer experts from the PCWorld staff who collectively have decades of experience testing and writing about all types of desktop PCs. Deals are hand-picked according to detailed analysis of historic pricing data and extensive knowledge of brand reliability and performance (i.e., the computers have to be good and the deals have to provide real value). It’s a great setup for everyday work, multitasking, and even some creative tasks. Just keep in mind that the 16GB of LPDDR5X RAM is soldered on and can’t be upgraded, so you’ll need to be comfortable with that amount for the long haul. Still, it’s a great desktop piece that not only looks good, but has the power under the hood to back it up as well. What are good websites to find computer deals? There are a ton of sites that sell computers, and scouring through all of them would take you a lot of time—that’s why we do it for you here and highlight the best deals we find. However, to save you some time and frustration, you need to be smart about where you look at any given time of the year. If you’re looking for a new computer during the holidays or around popular sale periods such as Black Friday or back-to-school, then you are likely to find great deals directly through first party vendor websites. These include the retail storefronts of popular computer manufacturers such as HP, Dell, and Lenovo. However, if you are looking in between sales periods, it’s generally a good idea to search through large third-party retailers such as Amazon, Adorama, Walmart, BestBuy, and Newegg. Oftentimes these websites will offer limited Deals of the Day type sales in hopes of getting rid of excess stock. On the upside, you can score still-decent PCs at a steep discount. When’s the best time to shop for a PC computer? Typically you’ll want to time your PC computer shopping around a prominent sales period. The biggest sales periods are Black Friday/Cyber Monday in late November and Amazon Prime Day in early-to-mid July. The best sales often occur leading up to and during these two events and they are great times to snag a new PC computer for cheap. Other holiday shopping periods such as the New Year sales in January, President’s Day sales in February, and the back-to-school sales event in August are also good times to find discounts on computers. What type of desktop should I get? You’ll see a ton of options when searching for a desktop computer, but they all mainly fit into four main categories: productivity tower PCs, gaming PCs, mini PCS, and all-in-ones (AiO). Which you should end up buying is entirely dependent upon what your needs are and what you want to do with your computer. If you are looking for something that will work in a home office or family room, then a productivity PC or AiO with a solid CPU and lots of RAM and storage is probably the way to go. If gaming is your main concern, a gaming PC can offer a lot more bang for your buck than a laptop and you should focus on getting the best GPU possible. Or if you just want something that can fit anywhere and provide basic computing then a mini PC is a good bet. What CPU and GPU should I get? When looking at your new computer’s CPU, get at least an Intel Core i5 or AMD Ryzen 5, both of which will provide plenty of processing power for everyday computing tasks. If you don’t intend to do any PC gaming, then feel free to save some money by going with integrated graphics. However, if you are looking to get your game on, we recommend at least an Nvidia GeForce 3060 or AMD Radeon RX 6600 XT, as these are the least expensive discrete graphics cards that can handle ray tracing well. If you aren’t interested in those cutting-edge lighting effects, however, the RTX 3050 and Radeon RX 6600 also provide decent 1080p gaming performance at even lower prices. The RTX 5070 is a strong midrange card that will allow for high settings at 1440p while the RTX 5080 is capable of decent 4K gaming if that’s more your speed. For those who won’t compromise for anything besides the best, the RTX 5090 is really your only option currently. How much memory and storage does my PC need? As for RAM, we think its best to shoot for 16GB at the minimum for productivity and gaming, but for family computers and internet browsing, 8GB should suffice. Storage size is dependent upon your personal needs, but it is generally a good idea to opt for an SSD over an standard HDD as they are much faster and don’t significantly affect the price of a desktop. Before deciding, it’s best to consider what your intended use of the computer will be. Are you just doing work or web browsing? Then something like 512GB will be plenty. If you want to load up a lot of large files such as games or content creation projects, then you’ll need at least 1 or 2TB or storage. However, just remember that even if your computer doesn’t have enough storage built-in you can always upgrade your SSD or go with an external drive to increase your available storage options. Is it a good idea to buy a refurbished computer? Refurbished computers are used machines that have been repaired, upgraded, and cleaned for the purpose of reselling. They’re usually open-box returns, overstock, or models with minor cosmetic damage (scratches, scuffs, etc). Refurbished computers can be a bargain hunter’s dream as they’re likely still in good (or great) condition and you can save a lot of money. That being said, refurbished computers can have their downsides as well. In addition to cosmetic blemishes, some of the internal components might be a little older or outdated and they might not be in peak condition due to previous usage. If you do consider buying a refurbished computer I recommend looking at eBay as they offer a one-year warranty. You can also check out manufacturer’s retail storefronts like Dell’s Outlet Store and Apple’s Refurbished Store—just be sure to look at the terms of warranty offered before purchasing.

item.title: SALES: PeakDo's New Battery for Starlink Mini Dish Features Fan, Puncture-Resistance
item.description:

PeakDo, which makes battery accessories for the portable Starlink Mini dish, has a new “Ultra” tier model with a built-in fan to keep the battery bank cool. The Chinese company today announced the LinkPower Ultra battery bank, which snaps onto the back of the Starlink Mini, giving owners a way to use the satellite internet service on the go. This is the fourth entry in the LinkPower series. One of the main enhancements to the Ultra is the “active cooling” on the battery, which seems to address user complaints about earlier LinkPower models overheating, especially on hot, sunny days outdoors. But in PeakDo’s case, the company says its semi-solid-state technology “enhances cell stability and thermal safety while reducing the risk of electrolyte leakage. Even if the cell is punctured under extreme conditions, it helps reduce the risk of thermal runaway, providing greater safety and reliability for outdoor use.” The battery’s higher density also enabled PeakDo to create a slightly thinner design for the Ultra model. The device is 22 millimeters (0.866 inches) thick, down from 27mm on other models. Despite its smaller size, the Ultra can still run for up to 5.5 hours on a single charge from its 27,000mAh battery, matching the performance of the LinkPower 3, which has a 27,500mAh battery. item.title: SALES: What sorcery is this? Telstra actually has some excellent NBN deals
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
As a lover of all things NBN, I’m no stranger to the latest internet deals in Australia. More often than not, it’s the same handful of internet service providers that jostle for my top recommendation — those being Exetel, Kogan Internet, Superloop and Spintel, to name a few. One provider that, if my memory serves correctly, has never popped up on my radar is Telstra. Yes, despite dominating the NBN landscape with a 35.2% market share, Telstra isn’t exactly known for its affordability. In actuality, the nation’s flagship telco is often the most expensive of the 30 or so providers I monitor on a regular basis. Imagine my surprise when I learned that Telstra, of all companies, had actual deals on its NBN lineup, with up to AU$240 in savings over six months! And while they still don’t offer the cheapest NBN plans, they’re still worth shouting about if you’re in the market for a new NBN plan. What’s more, Belong, a generally more affordable NBN provider 100% owned by Telstra, also has some attractive deals right now, including laying claim to the cheapest introductory cost on the NBN 100/500 tier at AU$59/m. Do note that the most affordable Telstra NBN plans require you to BYO modem. If you want a Telstra Smart Modem 4, you’ll not only need to pay more each month, but you’ll also need to pay any remaining device payments if you cancel your plan within 24 months. Alternatively, you can buy the Telstra modem for a one-off fee of AU$360. However, for that money, I would recommend seeking out one of the best mesh Wi-Fi systems in Australia instead. Shaving AU$30 off each month for the first six months, Telstra’s NBN 500 becomes a lot more attractive. Yes, it’s possible to spend less, but the fact that it comes in under the current average introductory cost of AU$74 is something to take notice of. Plus, the ongoing cost of AU$99 is roughly on par with the AU$95 average. Alternatively, for AU$10 less each month for the first half-year, you can get Belong’s NBN 500 plan. This is the current cheapest introductory cost of any provider, and it even includes a free SIM card to access the Telstra Wholesale network, loaded with AU$80 credit. The other speed tier where Belong claims the cheapest introductory cost is NBN 50, making it a tempting proposition for anyone who can comfortably get by with a slower connection. Of course, for just AU$4 more you could get the NBN 500 plan above (or NBN 100 if that’s the maximum available to you), which only highlights how much of a good deal it is. Telstra vs Belong: what’s the difference? Belong is 100% owned by Telstra and is a lower-cost alternative to the flagship brand. To offer more affordable mobile and NBN plans compared to Telstra, it makes some compromises where features and network coverage are concerned. In the case of mobile, Belong uses the Telstra Wholesale Network, which is said to cover around 98.8% of the population, compared to the full Telstra network that enjoys 99.7% coverage. In the case of NBN, however, both providers use the same underlying fixed-line network, so coverage isn't a differentiating factor. Actual speeds can still vary between providers, depending on how much capacity they have available and how their networks are managed, particularly during busier periods. However, there's no guarantee Telstra will deliver faster speeds than Belong on an equivalent plan. Belong keeps its costs lower by making some trade-offs, including giving customers the option to bring their own modem or purchase one separately. In either case, there’s no option for installation help. Telstra also supports BYO modems, but offers its own Smart Modem with 4G backup, a feature Belong doesn't provide. There are also some differences with technical support. Telstra offers 24/7 phone support and live chat, and has physical stores. Belong works on a digital-only basis, with support limited to online chat or messages via the website or app. There is limited phone support should you need it.

item.title: SALES: The 15 Best Deep-Cut Movies Coming Back to Theaters Soon
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
At some point, we’ve all had the same thought. We’re watching a movie either at home, on a plane, or at a friend’s, and we think, “I wish I had seen this in a theater.” Sometimes, we missed it because the movie came out years before our time. Other times, it’s because it wasn’t fully appreciated upon release. But we all have those titles we’d give anything to go back and see in a theater, which is what Regal is making possible starting this week. The theater chain just announced a new series called “Deep Cuts” featuring films that “deserve a second look from moviegoers in a theatrical environment.” Films that, according to Regal, “have developed a devoted following away from the big screen.” It’s a wild, wild list, including a few all-time classics, some serious deep cuts, lots of underappreciated gems, and even some hilarious wild cards. You can see the full list below (and at this link, along with tickets), but first, here are 15 that we’d very easily put down some cash to see, and think you should, too. Oldboy (November 1) A film so famous, so fucked up, and so fantastic that Spike Lee remade it with Josh Brolin just 10 years after its initial release. The original, which Regal is screening, is from director Park Chan-wook, who continues to make incredible movies like Decision to Leave and No Other Choice. Oldboy, however, follows a man who is mysteriously imprisoned for 15 years and seeks revenge upon release. But that’s just the start of the madness. Oh, and you can ignore that Lee remake. It’s bad. Under the Skin (November 6) These days, we generally think of Scarlett Johansson as a blockbuster superstar, and rightfully so. Her films have made billions. Which, thankfully, afforded her the ability to do this dark, disturbing, but beautiful sci-fi film from director Jonathan Glazer (The Zone of Interest). In it, Johansson plays an alien who makes her way through some harrowing human experiences. It’s a tough watch, but a very rewarding one. Zathura (November 6) Imagine if Jumanji was set in space and directed by Jon Favreau. Well, you don’t have to imagine. That film exists, and it’s called Zathura. Like Jumanji, it too is based on a book by Chris Van Allsburg (and some people even tangentially consider it to be part of that cinematic universe), but we think Zathura is even better than its more famous counterpart. Favreau delivers the type of whimsy and adventure he’d later bring to Marvel and Star Wars, and let’s face it: space is just cooler than the jungle. Bound (November 11) Before they brought us to incredible sci-fi worlds with The Matrix franchise, Cloud Atlas, and more, the Wachowskis rose to fame with this smart, sexy 1996 thriller. Jennifer Tilly and Gina Gershon star as budding lovers who conspire to steal millions from the mafia. And while it sounds simple, it’s as layered, powerful, and entertaining as everything the Wachowskis would do later. Repo Man (November 17) Alex Cox’s 1984 punk, sci-fi film Repo Man is perfectly of its time. It’s a film that very, very few people saw in the theaters but, in the era of VHS, eventually became one of those movies film fans watched again and again because it’s just so delightfully inventive. At its most basic, the film follows Emilio Estevez as a kid who finds himself working for a repo company looking for a car that’s hiding some aliens. It’s weird, it’s wacky, it’s wonderful. The General (November 19) If you actually saw The General in theaters when it came out, congratulations. You might be one of the oldest people on the planet. Buster Keaton’s signature comedy was released in 1926, so yes, it’s celebrating its 100th birthday this year. And yet, when you watch it, it works just as well as a movie that came out this year, and is somehow even more fascinating. Keaton’s performance as a Confederate train engineer in love paints a complex snapshot of the Civil War era, which is then bolstered by the film’s incredible, and hilarious, practical effects (because there were no other options). Truly an all-time classic that very few people get a chance to see in theaters. Vanilla Sky (November 21) Tom Cruise starring in surprising sci-fi movies has been in the news of late, which makes it a perfect time to revisit Vanilla Sky. Directed by Almost Famous helmer Cameron Crowe, this adaptation of a Spanish film features Cruise as a man left with severe facial injuries after an accident. He’s given a new face and, afterwards, begins to see and experience things he shouldn’t, which opens the door to all sorts of shocking things. The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift (November 22) Of all the Fast and Furious films, Tokyo Drift is my favorite. Is it the best? No. Is it the biggest? Definitely not. But it is the most relatable in that it’s (almost) a wholly separate story about a young kid who goes to a foreign country and gets wrapped up in its culture. Second to maybe only the original, it’s also the Fast and Furious movie that’s most in love with its cars. Plus, it’s the installment that brought Justin Lin into the franchise, which ended up working out well. Just an excellent time from beginning to end. The World’s End (November 23) The final film in Edgar Wright’s Cornetto Trilogy tells the story of Gary King (Simon Pegg). Gary is a man who peaked in high school and, years later, rounds up his old friends to relive the glory days by doing a massive bar crawl… which is when the aliens invade. Like Shaun of the Dead and Hot Fuzz before it, The World’s End is funny, exciting, and awesome. Where it differs, though, besides its genre, is how its exploration of nostalgia and addiction has become increasingly poignant, making it the perfect ending to an all-timer of a series. Blade II (November 24) Someone out there at some point has definitely said: “I wish Guillermo del Toro would make a Marvel movie.” And that person is in luck because the Oscar-winning director of Pan’s Labyrinth and The Shape of Water did just that back in 1998. It’s called Blade II, and it features Wesley Snipes’ vampire-killing anti-hero in an even more kinetic, action-packed sequel. Cowboys and Aliens (November 25) Of the nearly three dozen movies Regal is bringing back for its “Deep Cuts” series, we think this one stands alone. Why? Because despite the film’s incredible star power both in front of and behind the camera, we don’t think there’s really a world where it isn’t seen for what it is: a bad movie. But we do understand the desire to potentially perform a historical revision on that. We’ll never quite understand how a sci-fi western starring Han Solo and James Bond, directed by Jon Favreau and co-written by Damon Lindelof, is bad. Surely it has to have some merit, right? Well, you can find out on November 25, if you dare. Howard the Duck (November 26) “Imagine if George Lucas made a Marvel movie.” Well, again, he did. It was after Star Wars, in 1986, and it was called Howard the Duck. Unfortunately for Lucas, who produced the film, Howard the Duck is infamously one of the biggest flops in history and widely considered to be a huge piece of crap. And yet, 40 years after release, there is now plenty of nostalgic camp to it, especially since we’d imagine almost none of you saw it in a theater. So watching the awkwardness of Lea Thompson and a duck falling in love in a full theater will surely be a good time. Gremlins 2: The New Batch (November 27) If nothing else, Gremlins 2: The New Batch is worth seeing just to revel in the fact that everything about its iconic Key and Peele sketch is actually true. Joe Dante’s 1990 sequel to his 1984 hit is completely crazy, and we love it for that. Plus, Warner Bros. is working on another one, so it’s a good time to revisit the world of Mogwai and Gremlins. Addams Family Values (November 27) “They do what they want to do, say what they want to say, live how they want to live, play how they want to play, dance how they wanna dance, kick and they slap a friend: The Addams Family!” Such are the poetic lyrics of the legendary MC Hammer and his song, “Addams Groove,” which was released as part of this 1993 sequel to the 1991 hit film. The fact that Hammer did a song for the film speaks to not just how insanely ’90s this movie is, but how popular the original movie made The Addams Family at the time, necessitating this sequel. We’d imagine watching it in a theater is akin to jumping in a time machine. Waterworld (November 28) In 2026, the idea of studios losing hundreds of millions of dollars on ill-conceived blockbusters is almost par for the course. But for those of us alive in 1995, seeing it happen to this Kevin Costner sci-fi action-adventure felt wholly surprising. The idea of a world covered in water is so cool. Costner was such a big star. And it was, reportedly, the most expensive movie ever at the time. But all the elements (pun intended) never quite came together, and today, the film stands as a monument to a different era of filmmaking. It’s visually extraordinary. The rest of it? Not so much. And, again, that’s less than half the full offerings. Regal is also bringing back Martin Scorsese’s After Hours, the incredible documentary American Movie, Jim Henson’s iconic The Dark Crystal, Ryan Gosling’s awesome Drive, and much more. The full list is below, and tickets are available here.
