item.title: SALES: The best restaurants in India, ranked 1–50
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
The Condé Nast Traveller x District Top Restaurant Awards just wrapped, and the list of the best restaurants in India for 2026 is now out. The seventh edition of the awards was powered by VISA, and this year's list captures both continuity and change. The Condé Nast Traveller x District Top Restaurant Awards 2026 were revealed at a fabulous ceremony in Goa at The Grand Hyatt, Bambolim, where India's best restaurants, and the people behind them, were celebrated in style. The ranking of the top 50 restaurants in India has become a definitive barometer of the country's dining scene, tracking how chefs, bartenders, and restaurateurs are shaping the way India eats and drinks today. This year, Mumbai and Goa share the top spot, each placing 13 restaurants among the top fifty. Bengaluru follows with six, while Chennai and Kolkata hold four apiece. New Delhi takes three, and Shillong doubles its presence with two. The remaining five spots belong to Kasauli, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Gurugram and Karaikudi, each claiming one. Together, the spread marks a shift from past years. Goa has pulled level with Mumbai for the first time, a sign of just how much the state's dining scene has matured beyond its reputation as a holiday detour. How was this list made? Condé Nast Traveller curates an extensive shortlist of 1,000+ restaurants from across the country. Restaurants may nominate themselves to the list by filling up a form. 105 jury members, comprising India’s foremost tastemakers, undergo two phases of voting to come up with the 50 best restaurants in the country. Who decides the rankings? A 105-member jury privately voted for India’s best restaurants through a rigorous, two-phase process, with Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu India LLP as the process advisors. Jurors are screened for conflicts of interest, and regional diversity is built into the jury to ensure a balanced national view. Jurors include food critics, writers, chefs, fashion designers, artists, curators and others who know and love their food. Prateek Sadhu left the Kashmir Valley as a five-year-old in 1990, and NAAR, which means fire in Kashmiri, is where his search for home has landed, on the edge of a cliff near Darwa village in Himachal Pradesh. It seats just 16 in a cluster of wood and slate huts, and its six menus follow the Himalayas' six seasons, cooked by Sadhu and chef Kamlesh Negi over a juniper-smoked hearth. Getting here takes effort, about two and a half hours by road from Chandigarh, so plan a stop on the way. Ishar Sweets on the Kalka-Shimla Road is known for its kulfi and kalakand, and a box of either will earn you a warm welcome from the team. Sadhu once called opening NAAR "jumping without a parachute." This year, it landed at number one. Address: Amaya, VPO, Darwa, Kasauli, Himachal Pradesh 173236, India The Table has been a Mumbai landmark since 2011, and head chef Louis Gomes, who started here as a line cook over 15 years ago, now anchors a kitchen that balances institutions like the SoBo Salad and smoked goose-fat pâté with riskier dishes like lamb brain and morel vol-au-vent. Chef Will Aghajanian led its boldest reset in 2023. There's also a tasting menu that isn't printed anywhere. Ask for Chef's Picks if you arrive for an early dinner between 6:30 and 7pm, and the kitchen will put together six courses of snacks and small plates for Rs.4,200 a person, available for tables of two to four. Address: Kalapesi Trust Building, opposite Dhanraj Mahal, Apollo Bandar, Colaba, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400001, India Papa's seats only 12 people, and those seats are gone within a minute of being released each month. Up a narrow staircase above a Bandra sandwich shop, chef Hussain Shahzad runs a 12-course menu that plays by no fine-dining rules, with a Kashmiri Wellington, char siu pork in a modak and the Bugs Bunny dish, ants included. The tables come with built-in fidget spinners, and general manager Madhusudhan Kashyap sometimes pulls off card tricks between courses. The drinks are just as playful. The Papa's Classical Mix lists riffs on classic cocktails, and the Picante isn't on it, so ask for it anyway. It is a clear drink made with lemon and an in-house jalapeño marmalade, with a cleaner and brighter kick than the cloudy, coriander-heavy versions found elsewhere. Address: Waroda Road, Ranwar, Bandra West, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400050, India FarmLore sits at the end of the road out of Bengaluru, on 37 acres of mango and coconut groves that supply most of what ends up on the plate. The dining room seats just 18 and is lit by two wood stoves, Kannagi and Anjaneya, which burn mango wood cut from the property itself. Chef Johnson Ebenezer's tasting menu follows the farm's seasons, from charred lettuce with smoked ghee to lamb cooked for 18 hours with horsegram, and a few bolder dishes use the farm's own fire ants and Rameshwaram lobster. If you want to see where the experimenting happens, ask about Omnisense, the private dining room that connects directly to the R&D kitchen, where the team tests dishes that haven't reached the main menu yet. Address: Survey No. 67, Mohan Raju Layout, Sathanur Village, Bagalur Post, Bengaluru North Taluk, Karnataka 562149, India Sienna began in 2010 as a Shantiniketan pottery store and has grown into one of Kolkata's most compelling cultural projects, built around Bengal's maati and manush, its land and its people. The café's menu draws on the city's markets and kitchens, with dishes like bhetki à la Kiev made with radhuni butter and choto maach bhaja served with a fish egg aioli. It debuted on this list at number five in 2023. If you are dining alone, ask for the omakase experience. It isn't on the menu, but the kitchen will send out smaller portions so you can try more of the à la carte menu without filling up on rice. Address: 49/1, Golpark, Hindustan Park, Gariahat, Kolkata, West Bengal 700029, India Izumi's Goa outpost sits inside Botanique, a lush boutique guesthouse in Assagao, and brings the Mumbai original's attention to technique to an indoor-outdoor setting. That rigour comes from chef Nooresha Kably, who trained at the Tokyo Sushi Academy and a ramen school in Yokohama before building Izumi. It shows most clearly in the sushi, where the nigiri is made with Japanese rice sourced from Himachal and is meant to be eaten by hand. A separate yakitori bar sits alongside the main menu. For something off it, ask chef Raffael Kably to make his spicy prawn yaki udon. If there is hamachi collar in the kitchen that day, ask him to grill it for you. Address: 45, Mapusa, Anjuna, Chapora Road, Assagao, Bardez, Goa 403507, India Indian Accent opened in 2009 and changed how India thinks about its own cuisine, moving dining out well beyond butter chicken and Mughlai staples with dishes like the blue cheese naan, pork ribs glazed in meetha achaar and a kala khatta sorbet served in a miniature pressure cooker. It has since moved from The Manor to The Lodhi, and chef Shantanu Mehrotra, who has been with the restaurant since day one, now leads the kitchen. The tasting menu shows the kitchen at its most inventive. Ask for tables 26 or 27, which overlook the glass room and are favourites with celebrities and VIPs, as much for the play of sun or moonlight on the water as for the people-watching. If there's a dish from an older menu you've always wanted to try, call at least 24 hours ahead and the team can recreate it from their archive. Address: The Lodhi, Lodhi Road, New Delhi 110003, India Chef-owner Bawmra Jap, a Kachin from Myanmar, has run Bomras in Anjuna for 16 years, building a following on tea leaf salad, tiger prawn ceviche sharpened with local lime, and a smoked pork fried rice regulars won't share. The restaurant shut briefly during the pandemic and reopened in 2020 at a new Anjuna address with a small herb garden feeding the kitchen, and the loyal crowd came right back, Ed Sheeran included. What doesn't make the printed menu is worth asking about. Jap often cooks for friends off-menu, dishes like spicy chicken feet salad, slow-roasted pig's cheek, or bamboo shoots with wood ear mushrooms, and it's worth checking what he's made that day rather than assuming it's not on offer. Sundays bring a different kind of experiment, with the chef running through vegetable, chicken and prawn khowsuey variations. The tender coconut panna cotta with passion fruit remains the constant, and one of Goa's most reliable desserts. Address: 1152, opp. Our Lady Of Health Chapel, Mazal Waddo, Anjuna, Goa 403509, India Avartana opened in 2017 and has spent the years since turning South Indian food into a tasting menu experience without losing what makes it South Indian in the first place. The name is Sanskrit for rhythm and repetition, and that logic runs through four menus of increasing length. The seven-course Maya, nine-course Bela, eleven-course Jiaa and thirteen-course Anika. Bottle gourd is served as marinated spirals with plum chutney and rice crisps, parotta is compressed into a single bite with coconut chicken and a toffee made from Uthukuli butter, and the double-distilled rasam alone has diners asking if they can take a bottle home. All menus can be adjusted for dietary restrictions and preferences, and for a special occasion the kitchen will also put together personalised menu cards, complete with your name and an illustration based on your photo. Address: ITC Grand Chola, Little Mount, Guindy, Chennai, Tamil Nadu 600032, India Website: itchotels.com/in/en/itcgrandchola-chennai At The Bombay Canteen, servers read the room and start guiding your order before you have even opened the menu, and the whole floor works in a kind of unspoken choreography. Chef Gaurav Yadav now leads the kitchen, and he has kept a decade of signatures alive, including eggs Kejriwal and the gulab nut doughnut, while adding newer dishes like chicken jhol momos. If you are dining solo or visiting for the first time, sit at the bar. It is easy to walk up to, and the bartenders are happy to recommend their own favourite spots around the city. If you cannot decide what to order, ask for the Canteen Experience, a tasting menu of six to eight courses that samples the kitchen's range in smaller portions. Time a washroom trip for a loop of 70s and 80s Bollywood hits playing against the art-deco tiling. Before you leave, ask for the restaurant's Mumbai checklist map, a list of old-guard eateries across the city that includes Ling's Pavilion and Trishna. Address: Unit-1, Process House, S.B. Road, Kamala Mills, Near Radio Mirchi Office Lower, Parel, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400013, India Masque has become the country's most visible face of modern Indian fine dining, led by chef Varun Totlani, who joined as a commis and rose to head chef in 2022. After a decade in its original Shakti Mills warehouse, the restaurant has been completely rejigged, and walking in now feels like stepping into a new place altogether. The new room looks like Gotham City meets art deco, and the kitchen, once hidden, is now visible from the dining room. The 10-course tasting menu still draws on ingredients foraged across the country, from Himachal ferns to Ladakh apricots, and mid-meal, guests step into the kitchen for a counter course. The menu is less fixed than it looks, too. If there's a dish from a past menu you're craving, mention it when you book, and the kitchen will often work it back in. One regular arranged an entire baby shower meal built around his wife's favourite dishes from old menus, and another guest bought out Masque Lab to cook alongside Totlani himself. For more privacy, ask about the table in the newly refurbished wine cellar, though like the old table at the pass, it isn't something you can simply book. It comes down to a conversation with the team. Address: Unit G3, Shakti Mills, Off Dr E Moses Road, Mahalaxmi, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400011, India Chef Alexander Lee Sanchez opened Americano in Kala Ghoda in 2019 with partner Mallyeka Watsa, and by 9pm most nights the place runs like a sold-out concert, with Sanchez himself working the pass at the centre of the room. The cooking is modern Italian with no gimmicks, built on ingredients tested until they earn their place on the plate. Pizza is the obsession here. The dough has been perfected over years and the toppings are balanced with real precision, resulting in what is arguably the best slice in the city, crisp at the edges and just charred enough. The roast chicken is simple and often overlooked, and the tiramisu has its own following, scooped fresh at the table over a layer of tempered chocolate. If you're celebrating something, give the team advance notice and they'll turn that same tiramisu into a full birthday cake, made and served the same way. Address: 121/123 Radha Bhavan, Nagindas Master Road, Kala Ghoda, Fort, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400001, India INJA, tucked into The Manor, is chef Adwait Anantwar's Indian-Japanese experiment, and it has split Delhi between those who call it genius and those who call it sacrilege. Anantwar spent three and a half years testing the pairings, which produced a chawanmushi spiked with rasam masala, gobi 65 rolled as a maki, and gajar ka halwa tucked inside a steamed bun, all without any soy sauce in the kitchen. The Japanese bhel is a favourite with regulars, who ask for it by name because it is on the menu but not always available. The bar is worth the same attention. Mixologist Supradeep makes off-menu cocktails, including a Gondhoraj Margarita with blanco tequila, yuzu bitters and Gondhoraj lemons sourced from Bengal. Design lovers should also ask to see the PDR, where the dining table is a single six-foot slab of pink marble. Address: The Manor, 77 Friends Colony West, New Delhi 110065, India Amar Khamar's Lunch Room grew out of the founders' earlier venture, Annaja, and now serves home-style Bengali food across a 20-seat space in Ballygunge. Founded in 2019 by Sujoy Chatterjee to support small farmers, the restaurant sources heirloom rice, lentils and spices from growers across West Bengal, and its signature Chhuti-r Bhat, a four-course holiday meal on a banana leaf, is built around lesser-known heirloom rice rather than the usual Gobindobhog. The mutton dish, Chui Jhal Mangsho, gets its heat the old way, from the stems of the chui jhal vine rather than chillies. Fish those stems out and chew them between bites of meat for a slow, smoky burn instead of an upfront one. Address: 21B, Hindustan Rd, Ballygunge, Kolkata, West Bengal 700029, India NĀVU is a small, chef-led restaurant where Pallavi Mithika Menon and Kanishka Sharma run short, seasonal menus that play with the classics. Their chicken liver pâté comes donburi-style over miso butter rice and lap cheong, a pairing that shouldn't work but does. Recent menus have included mustard ice cream with pickled cherry tomatoes and beef tartare with sunchoke purée, while the cauliflower crème brûlée has survived every change. Look for the cranes, a motif borrowed from Japanese mythology and reworked into NĀVU's own emblem. They appear on the menu, in the décor and sometimes on the table, and the dishes marked with a crane icon are the way in. If you want to know the story behind them, ask for Chef Kanishka, and you might leave with a crane of your own. Address: IndiQube Symphony, Shankarnarayan Building, MG Road, Ashok Nagar, Bengaluru, Karnataka 560025, India The Second House sits in a 108-year-old Indo-Portuguese bungalow in Saligao, designed by architect Ayaz Basrai to feel like a home crossed with a contemporary art gallery. Chef Jyoti Singh, previously of O Pedro, runs a menu shaped by his time in Egypt and Indonesia, including a house bread that merges Goan poee with Egyptian baladi bread and a riff on balchao with Indonesian flavours. One dish stays off the menu entirely. The Midnight Noodle, a beef and mushroom noodle with a satisfying chew, is a nostalgic late-night dish that Jyoti only makes for people he knows. Address: Muddavaddi, Saligao, Goa 403511, India Theta Theta Telugu comes from Sampath Tummala, whose family runs the Hyderabad institution The Spicy Venue, and chef Vignesh Ramachandran, previously of Indian Accent, and it reworks Telugu classics through techniques borrowed from Spain, France, Italy, West Asia and Burma. The tur dal and mango pickle of everyday Telugu meals becomes Mudapappu Hummus, topped with a kalamata olive pickle flavoured like avakai, and ghee prawns arrive in a tamarind sauce alongside a curry leaf brioche. There is a table that regulars ask for by name. Table 21, tucked into a corner, is chef Vignesh's own table, and it is where you want to be if you'd rather eat with your hands away from the rest of the room. Dining solo or as a pair, ask for the community table instead, since it's the easiest way to see what everyone around you has ordered. Don't skip the mutton chops seena roast, which regulars stretch into a bigger plate by sharing it with bread, and pick up a few extra paan bonbons on your way out. Address: Road No. 10A, Gayatri Hills, Jubilee Hills, Hyderabad, Telangana 500045 Praça Prazeres is chef Ralph Prazeres and Stacy Gracias's restaurant in Panjim's Fontainhas quarter, set in a restored heritage home and built by the couple behind Padaria Prazeres. The menu draws on Ralph's years in kitchens from London to Copenhagen, with dishes like Scotch eggs, crisped pork belly with apple sauce and pan-roasted fish with beurre blanc. Much of the furniture came from his grandfather's home, and a live kitchen on the ground floor keeps the room intimate. Head upstairs to the attic bar for a cocktail or the in-house limoncello alongside a charcuterie board. If you go to the washroom, scan the QR code there, for a small Easter egg that captures the restaurant's playful side. Address: Off, Rua de Ourém, behind Hotel Sona Building, Altinho, Goa, Panaji, Goa 403001, India The Johri sits inside a 19th-century haveli in Jaipur's Johri Bazaar, its pink walls, latticed windows and hand-painted cranes making it one of the city's most striking dining rooms. Chef Sonu Kumar, building on frameworks laid down by chef Vikram Arora, runs a seasonal vegetarian menu rooted in Rajasthan's kitchens, from a paan-patta chaat with real heat to a truffle aloo tikki finished under a parmesan "papad" and a gold-leafed mirchi ka halwa that works for Jain diners too. The restaurant doubles as the dining room for a five-suite hotel, so the pace stays unhurried. The soundtrack is worth asking about. The playlist swings from Bappi Lahiri to Lifafa, and the team will share it on Spotify if you ask. Address: 3950, MSB Ka Rasta, Johri Bazar, Ghat Darwaza, Jaipur, Jaipur Nagar Nigam Area, Rajasthan 302003, India Chef Dhiraj Dargan built his reputation at Comorin by nudging familiar dishes sideways rather than reinventing them outright, slipping bakarwadi into kadhi, crisping gatte like polenta, and plating beetroot raita as a radial of pickled vegetables. A few old favourites have technically been discontinued but never really left the kitchen. The mutton tawa pulao can be made on request with no advance notice, while the meat-choley, a holdover from an old Ramzan menu, needs two days' notice to pull off. Regulars who miss a classic makhni on this otherwise unconventional menu can also ask for it, and there's a barley-quinoa salad the chef will build with chicken if you ask ahead. The bar, led by Varun Sharma, matches the kitchen's precision with clarified cocktails, sous-vide infusions and in-house bitters, while the zero-proof list, carrot shrub Bloody Marys and khus-and-basil sodas, holds its own rather than feeling like an afterthought. The space also runs as a small retail counter, so it's worth browsing the teas, ceramics and serveware on your way out. Address: 101, First Floor, Two Horizon Center, DLF Phase 5, Sector 43, Gurugram, Haryana 122009, India Kopitiam Lah in Indiranagar recreates the Malaysian coffee shop that anchors daily life in the country. It comes from pastry artist Joonie Tan, of Lavonne, and chef David D'Souza. Mornings here follow the old ritual of thick kopi with condensed milk, half-boiled eggs with soy and white pepper, and kaya toast with salted butter, alongside nasi lemak and laksa. Key ingredients like belacan and gula melaka are flown in to keep the flavours faithful. The egg tart is the one thing worth racing for. It arrives with a light pastry and a well-browned top, but the kitchen sends out only one batch a day and it is mostly gone by noon. Come early and order yours as soon as you sit down. Address: Ground Floor, 1088, 12th Main Rd, Doopanahalli, Indiranagar, Bengaluru, Karnataka 560008, India Chef Kavan Kuttappa's Naru began with DIY ramen kits during lockdown, moved through pop-ups and now runs as a 20-seat noodle bar inside The Courtyard in Shanti Nagar. The menu is short, with six ramens, a few sides and some sake, including a shoyu ramen with chashu pork, a creamy tori paitan and a Goan chorizo tantanmen. Getting a seat is the hard part. There are no walk-ins, and bookings open online every Monday at 8pm. Open the booking page in Google Chrome at 7.55pm with autofill switched on, decide your day in advance, and when the clock hits 8, move quickly through the pages, scan the QR code and pay. Address: 105, Kengal Hanumanthaiah Rd, Raja Ram Mohanroy Extension, Shanti Nagar, Bengaluru, Karnataka 560027, India Chef Avinash Martins builds his menu at Cavatina in Benaulim out of memory as much as training, drawing on his grandmother's negotiations with fish vendors and childhood afternoons spent waiting at the jetty for crabs. The food changes with the season, from valchi bhaji with mushrooms and morels to tongue in temperado masala reworked as tartare, and nothing on the plate is anonymous. Bamboo mats are woven by local artisans, masalas are ground by hand, and the bread comes from a village poder, all part of Martins's effort to keep Goa's small economies alive alongside its traditions. Sachin Tendulkar is a regular, and Coldplay has stopped by too. Ask for the chef's table and you'll be seated at a corner spot near the kitchen with a direct view of the pass, along with a couple of extras, including Avinash's favourite cocktail, which isn't on the menu but can be requested from Shubham at the bar. Visit at lunch and you might also get to try the staff meal of the day. Address: Taj Hotel Road, near Joecons Beach Resort, Benaulim, Goa 403716, India Kaspers is chef Will Aghajanian's Bandra bistro, and it's where he lets his freak flag fly. Aghajanian, culinary director at The Table, cooks classic bistro fare with a Bengali streak, using kasundi as a dijonnaise in dishes like the mud crab gratin with lamb brain. Artist Kacper Abolik painted the walls with cherubs, and the tables are covered in paper, so pick up a crayon. If your doodle inspires the team, they may frame it and hang it on the wall. Ask for the specials board before you open the menu, since the veal chop Cordon Bleu, the tandoori crab donostiarra and the chocolate chip cookie dough soufflé, which takes 25 minutes to make, tend to sell out. The zero-proof cocktails are all off-menu, so ask for those too. Address: Classic Corner, 7/8, St Andrews Rd, Bandra West, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400050, India Larder & Folk began in 2021 as a delivery and production kitchen in Mala, started by Priyanka Sardessai and her husband, Siddharth Sumitran, and has since grown into a full cafe in São Tomé. The space is filled with cat figurines, recipe books and potted plants. The menu covers hearty sandwiches, including a hot honey doughnut with fried chicken, stuffed bombolinis and Sardessai's cookies. Sundays are the best day to visit, because the display case fills with specials and the cakes, puffs and desserts change every week. Look out for the soft shell crab burger, which sells out quickly. If you bring a dog, they get a free recycled fabric tug toy from Maka Naka. Address: HO, 1/61, Vivenda Aleluia, Rua São Tomé, behind GPO, Panaji, Goa 403001, India Padaria Prazeres opened in Panjim in April 2021, when chef Ralph Prazeres and his wife, Stacy Gracias, returned to Goa from London. Ralph trained at Le Cordon Bleu and worked in kitchens including St John and Bao, with a stint at noma, while Stacy came from a career in finance. Their artisanal bakery and café is built on European traditions, and its pastel de nata, with flaky pastry and a rich egg custard, is what first made it famous. Seats fill up fast, so Ralph suggests arriving at 9am, when everything is freshly laid out and the room is calm. Come late in the day and the broken or slightly burnt palmiers are discounted. Address: Celeste Plaza, Ground floor, opposite Models Celebrity, Caranzalem, Panaji, Goa 403002, India Hosa occupies one of Siolim's prettiest Indo-Portuguese bungalows, with a powder-blue façade, a leafy patio and a bar lined with tinctures and infusions. Chef Harish Rao runs a 38-dish menu that moves across Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, from curry leaf-cured snapper in kokum rasa to almonds dressed up like chicken 65. Beverage director Varun Sharma, who also runs the bars at Comorin and Indian Accent, keeps the drinks just as inventive, including a shandy dispensed from a contraption on the table and a full section of zero-proof cocktails. Dosas are worth treating as more than a side for chutneys here. Ask your server what they would pair with them, since the friendly service team is happy to suggest curries, and pineapple gojju is a hot favourite. Address: House no.60/1, Irada Home, Vaddy, near St. Anthony’s Church, Siolim, Bardez, Goa 403517, India Grumps sits at the end of a winding path in Sangolda that seems to lead nowhere until the sign appears. It was founded by Kartik Vasudeva, formerly of The Bombay Canteen, and his partner Agrini Satyarthi, and it has become one of North Goa's most dependable neighbourhood bars. Drinks and food arrive fast, the staff remember faces, and solo diners are as welcome as groups. The menu is compact, with dishes like beef croquettes in star anise jus and Sichuan fried chicken, and the cocktails include a whiskey drink built on sweet bun syrup and oloroso sherry. Every guest leaves with a card of the team's favourite places to eat and drink across Goa, but the real value is in the follow-up. Ask Kartik or Agrini what to order at each spot on it, and they'll help you turn the card into a proper itinerary. Address: House No, 58 B, Grumps St, behind Chogm Road, Sangolda, Bardez, Goa 403511, India Chef Manoj Shetty runs the kitchen at Bandra Born day to day, while founder Gresham Fernandes, who also DJs, sets the wider direction and occasionally takes over the console himself on a good night. The food riffs on the suburb's mixed heritage rather than replicating it straight, so beets get cooked like steak and the East Indian crab curry turns up with croissant pav instead of the usual bread. Regulars have an advantage here. Call ahead and the kitchen will go off-menu or build around dietary needs, and the bar keeps a rotating set of seasonal cocktail specials that never make it onto the printed list, so it's worth asking what's currently pouring rather than sticking to the menu. Address: Rose Minar, 87, Chapel Rd, Annexe, Reclamation, Bandra West, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400050, India Rannaghor is the tasting room on the second floor of Sienna's century-old house in Hindustan Park, where chefs Avinandan Kundu and Koyel Roy Nandy serve a 13-course modern Bengali menu at a chef's table for eight. The team cooks, plates and explains every course, from a "Snacks-Jam" board of katla belly bacon and sting ray salami to a mutton rizala risotto finished with bone marrow butter. The plates are made at the restaurant's Shantiniketan studio. Many of the ingredients will be unfamiliar to non-Bengali diners, so ask about them. If you ask with a smile, the team will bring out samples to taste raw, including whole ants before they become chutney, monkey fruit, whey jaggery, dried mahua and radhuni seeds. Address: 49/1, Hindustan Park Rd, Golpark, Hindustan Park, Gariahat, Kolkata, West Bengal 700029, India Petisco is a three-storey gastrobar in Panjim, opened in 2020 by chefs Halton D'Souza and Pranav Dhuri, and each floor has its own mood. The middle level suits groups sharing plates, the top floor is better for dates, and the basement is where the night gets loud, with live gigs and karaoke. It is also the best place to sit. The basement has its own menu, and it is where you are most likely to find mixologist Dev Narvekar, whose cocktail list changes with the season. Pair the drinks with the seafood specials, since any special fish the kitchen finds in the market that day ends up on that menu. Address: Dr RS Rd, Opposite Municipal Garden, Altinho, Panaji, Goa 403001, India Rynsan is set in a restored Assam-style bungalow on the edge of Shillong, where musician Hammarsing Kharhmar and his wife, Riyaki Jana, cook from Garo, Khasi and Jaintia traditions, with nods to Nagaland, Mizoram, Burma and Thailand. The menu treats these as a conversation rather than a fusion, so wild fern salad sits beside smoked pork with perilla, and steamed rice cakes turn into sliders. The best way in is to ask questions. Ask what ingredient is in season and request an off-menu salad built around it, then try lesser-known produce like wild perilla, jaïur and kholar beans. Also ask for a taster of the local spirits, since many are made for Rynsan by Meghalaya's best brewers and aren't sold elsewhere in the city. Address: Boyce Road, 36, College, near Shillong, Laitumkhrah, Shillong, Meghalaya 793003, India The Bangala serves Chettinad food the way it has always been eaten, on banana-leaf plates at communal teak tables, in a heritage hotel dining hall in the heart of Karaikudi. The masalas are still hand-pounded, and dishes like uppu kari, made with mutton, shallots and gundu milagai chillies, show the cuisine's range beyond just heat. First-timers can find the customs a little confusing, so it helps to follow someone at the table who clearly knows the ritual, sprinkling water on the banana leaf and wiping it away before service starts. For a full breakdown, ask for F&B manager Arul Selvam or senior staff Chandran and Selvakumar, who speak English, or Raja for Hindi. At the end of the meal, fold the leaf back toward you, with the middle stem facing in, a small gesture that makes cleanup easier. Address: Devakottai Rd, Senjai, Karaikudi, Tamil Nadu 630001, India Ekaa's menu is cuisine-agnostic, built so that a single ingredient anchors each dish, which is what the name, meaning "the one," refers to. Chef Niyati Rao, who trained briefly at noma, and restaurateur Sagar Neve source locally and ferment in-house, and the cocktails draw on ingredients foraged from seven of India's ecosystems, including its mountains, oceans and the desert. The tasting menu, which leaves the evening entirely to the chef, is designed to surprise.. Ask for the Magic Cake and the team will take it from there, though it's best left unspoiled until it lands at your table. Address: 1st Floor, Kitab Mahal, D Sukhadwala Rd, Azad Maidan, Fort, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400001, India Trishna has been serving Konkani and Mangalorean seafood in Kala Ghoda since 1965, run by a family from Mangalore, and its butter pepper garlic crab has become something of a benchmark for the city. The room is small and the décor hasn't changed much over the decades, but that hasn't stopped it from drawing everyone from regulars to first-time visitors and the occasional celebrity. Beyond the crab, the rawas Hyderabadi, coated in black pepper and pan-seared until crisp outside and tender within, and the Koliwada prawns are worth ordering. It's the kind of place people plan their next visit to before dessert arrives at the first one. Address: 7, Sai Baba Mandir Marg, Kala Ghoda, Fort, Mumbai 400053 Aeseo is the first Korean restaurant to make this list. Chennai's Korean food scene dates back to the 1990s, when Hyundai set up a plant outside the city and a tight-knit Korean community built a dining culture that has stayed largely under the radar. Aeseo is part of that story. The kitchen is run entirely by a Korean team, the vegetables are grown locally. Every table has its own charcoal grill and a bell you can ring to call for more soju, beer or food without waiting to flag anyone down. The barbecue duck, grilled until the skin crisps and the meat nearly drips, is worth the trip to Chennai alone. For the full spread, order the makchang and dakgalbi gui off the grill, along with gimbap and saeu tuigim on the side. Address: 15, East Ave, Kesavaperumalpuram, Raja Annamalaipuram, Chennai, Tamil Nadu 600028, India Megu has been one of Delhi's most polished addresses for Japanese dining since 2012, and head chef Shubham Thakur now keeps its balance of restraint and luxury intact. Fish is flown in from Tokyo twice a week and served as nigiri, sashimi or carpaccio, alongside long-standing signatures like the crispy asparagus and tuna tataki with ponzu.The omakase room is lined with silk-clad red and pink walls, and one corner table looks out over a hidden zen garden. At the centre of the restaurant sits a crystal Buddha in a pool of water. Legend has it that if you pour water on the part of the Buddha that matches your ailment, you will be cured. Address: The Leela Palace New Delhi, Africa Ave, Diplomatic Enclave, Chanakyapuri, New Delhi, Delhi 110023, India La Loca María in Bandra is chef Manuel Olveira's tribute to his mother, who first put him to work in a kitchen in Toledo. The name means "the crazy Maria." Olveira trained in Michelin-starred dining rooms in Madrid before cooking in Dubai and Mumbai, and the restaurant brings that background together with a loud, generous energy. The menu runs from gambas al ajillo and charred octopus to lobster paella, with tacos that have become a favourite. There is also a dish you will only get if you ask for it. Olveira first made it for his nephew Shiv, layering the restaurant's carpaccio between two slices of Pan de Ajo, its garlic bread, and it has since become a family snack for the team. Ask for the Carpaccio a la Loca María in a Pan de Ajo. Address: Fatima villa, 29th Rd, Bandra West, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400050, India Kappa Chakka Kandhari has been on this list since it opened in 2018, and its menu still reads like a map of Kerala's toddy shops, home kitchens and temples. Chef Regi Mathew spent about three years travelling the state, speaking to more than 250 home cooks and 70 toddy shop owners, some of whom now cook in his kitchen. The result is dishes like prawn kizhi steamed in banana leaf, kudampuliyitta fish curry served with mashed tapioca, and mutton chaps with pathiri. The Cloud Pudding, a light tender coconut dessert, is the restaurant's best-known dish and often sells out before diners finish their meal. Reserve it as soon as you sit down, before you place the rest of your order. Address: 10, Haddows Rd, opp. Shastri Bhavan, Thousand Lights West, Nungambakkam, Chennai, Tamil Nadu 600006, India Baan PhadThai started in Bangkok in 2016, built around an 18-ingredient secret sauce for phad thai that earned it a spot on Bangkok's first Michelin Bib Gourmand list, a recognition it held for six years. The Bengaluru outpost, on Indiranagar's 12th Main, keeps the menu tight and the room spare, just 30 seats, green and brown tones, and a few vintage Thai posters. The food is curated for the Indian palate without losing its balance of sweet, sour, salty and spicy, from a raw papaya salad with roasted peanuts to a crabmeat omelette finished with a tom yum and kaffir lime reduction. The signature phad thai arrives on a banana leaf in an enamel bowl and gets tossed tableside, with a box of condiments on the side so you can adjust the sauce to taste. Once you book, the restaurant sends a Spotify playlist to the number on your reservation, ninety minutes of Thai disco, rock and molam curated by co-founder Sid Mewara, meant to get you in the mood for the meal on your way over. Address: Sai Suraksha, 1090, 12th Main Rd, Doopanahalli, Indiranagar, Bengaluru, Karnataka 560008, India Jamun in Assagao is the Goa outpost of a Delhi restaurant from Lodhi Colony, built around regional Indian cooking. Chef Rahul Gomes Pereira, known as Picu, runs a menu that pairs tandoor dishes like stuffed morels and beetroot and amaranth galouti with Goan plates such as crab kalchi kodi and pork assado. The cocktails lean on local ingredients, including the signature Jamun Sour and a Bombay Spritz made with bael flower. The restaurant is set in a 200-year-old Goan villa that works almost like a museum, so it pays to wander and ask questions. Ask your server to walk you through the house and the stories behind its objects, especially the chandelier made from old garrafões, the traditional feni bottles. The ceiling had to be reinforced to carry their weight. Address: 190, Mazal Vado, Assagao, Goa 403507, India Chef Manu Chandra's return to Bengaluru in 2023 is LUPA, an 11,000sqft Italian-villa fantasy on MG Road with a salumeria, a gelato lab and a wine cellar 12 feet underground. The kitchen leans on generosity and rigour, from Parma ham with warm tigelle buns to a steak tartare mixed tableside and oxtail ravioli that breaks open into bone marrow broth. A new menu launched in June, but the service is what sets the restaurant apart. Repeat guests are matched with their favourite servers and given personalised recommendations. First-timers should ask for operations manager Tanmoy, bar lead Mo, or seniors Suman, Dhruv and Monsoon, all of whom Chandra encourages to read the room and take ownership of the table. Address: Ground Floor, NO.86, SPENCER'S TOWERS, Mahatma Gandhi Rd, Haridevpur, Shanthala Nagar, Ashok Nagar, Bengaluru, Karnataka 560001, India Trèsind arrived in BKC in 2018 as the Mumbai outpost of the Dubai-born group behind Trèsind Studio, the first Indian restaurant in the world to hold three Michelin stars. Chef Sarfaraz Ahmed leads the kitchen here, building on techniques developed under group corporate chef Himanshu Saini, and the tasting menu moves through the country's regional flavours with dishes like Khichdi of India, a dish so central to the brand that taking it off the menu would reportedly start a fight among regulars. Guests are welcomed with hot towels and a calming aroma pot before eating much of the meal with their hands. The team pays close attention to regulars, not just their names but where they're from, and will sometimes call out a mix-in for the khichdi tied to a diner's home state. There's a quieter gesture too. Come in wearing black, and your white napkin will quietly be swapped for one that matches. Address: Ground Floor Inspire BKC E, G Block BKC, Bandra Kurla Complex, Bandra East, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400051, India Chef Niyati Rao's Nonna Mei, on the first floor of The Shillong Address, is built on the idea that an Italian nonna and a Khasi mei cook in much the same way, with great produce, inherited technique and plenty of love. Rao spent nearly two years on research, finding local ingredients like the tomatoes she calls "magic soil" produce, building a supply chain of Meghalaya farmers and working with the town's only cheesemaker. The sourdough, which is the base for the bread and pizzas, is fed by Shuruwat, the starter carried over from Ekaa. Behind the menu sits a rotating collection of ferments, pickles and dry-aged meats, from lacto-fermented Khasi tomatoes to house-cured lardo and pickled jyllang, or garlic chives. Ask about what is on hand that month and taste a little of what the kitchen builds its dishes from. Address: 1st Floor, The Shillong Address, Police Bazar, Shillong, Meghalaya 793001, India Mister Merchant's is a Pune import that has settled in Mapusa, built around the story of an imagined, well-travelled Parsi merchant whose journeys through Persia and the Levant shaped the menu. The interiors follow the same idea, filled with maps and lamps. Chef Rahul Pereira's food traces the Silk Route with an Indian accent, from saffron chicken cigars and mushroom and truffle baklava to a thecha and curry leaf hummus. Goan touches appear too, including a slow-cooked pork vindaloo and the richly spiced Merchant's Mutton Curry. Zero-waste cocktails infused with walnut and curry leaf round things out. Regulars also know to ask about the slow-cooked bone broth, which the team serves in a warm cup every now and then. Address: 501, Calizor, Alto De Lourdis, House No, Moide, Mapusa, Goa 403508, India O Pedro in BKC feels like a Goan living room dropped into the middle of Mumbai's business district, with a bar that holds its own. The menu is best treated as a starting point. Ask for Pedro's Favourites, a tasting menu the team builds around your preferences, running from Goa's lesser-known vegetarian dishes to fresh seafood. Then ask what has just come out of the wood-fire oven that day and choose how it is cooked, whether Recheado, Cafreal or Portuguese-style chilli-garlic. The same oven bakes the poees and the pastéis de nata, so save room for both. The restaurant also hosts guest shifts from Goan kitchens like Hosa and Grumps, which keeps the programme changing. Address: Jet Airways, Laxmi Tower, Godrej BKC, Plot No C-68, G Block BKC, Bandra Kurla Complex, Bandra East, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400051, India Seefah is a Thai and Japanese restaurant on Bandra's Hill Road, run by chefs and co-owners Seefah Ketchaiyo and Karan Bane, who bring about 30 years of kitchen experience between them. The two menus are entirely separate, so it works like two restaurants under one roof. Try the raw papaya salad and Khao Kluk Ka-Pi, a stir-fried rice with shrimp, pork and raw mango, then come back for the Japanese side, or ask the team what they recommend that day and build a meal across both. The cocktail menu is excellent, with a Som Tam-infused gin drink named after the restaurant. Scan the QR code on it for a small guide to Bangkok and Tokyo. Address: 2 Floor, Khan House, 201, Hill Rd, above McDonald's, Ranwar, Bandra West, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400050, India The Farm began as a family farm started in 1974 by Arul Futnani's father, and in 2009, Arul and his business partner Shalini Phillips opened a restaurant and food store on the land in Semmancheri. Almost everything on the menu is grown, raised or made on-site, from the cheeses to the sausages and ketchup, and what isn't comes from local fishermen or small producers nearby. The setting feels more like a picnic than a restaurant, with tables under a roofed area facing the wood-fired oven, or out in the garden among the farm's own animals. Start with the Dalle-Chhurpi-Toast and smoked pork, and order the Masala Fish Fry with Chatti Choru if you want something more comforting. The wood-fired pizzas can be made with two different toppings, one on each half, if you ask. Finish with the Old Fashioned Chocolate Cake. Address: 1-277, Rajiv Gandhi Salai, Semmancheri, Egattur, Chennai, Tamil Nadu 600119, India For the Record, known to locals as FTR, feels less like a bar than the home of a friend who collects vinyl, bakes sourdough and builds his own speakers. That friend is Buland Shukla, an architect, audio engineer and musician, and his Panjim bar folds cocktails, food and music into one experience. The drinks are short in number and built on local spirits, including agave with bimli fruit poached in toddy vinegar, and most nights bring a vinyl listening session, a swing evening or a set by his Banjara Quartet. Stay long enough and you may find your way to Off The Record, an extension of the bar tucked between the counter and the backstage, where after-hours guests can make a drink of their own, draw, put on a record or simply hang out with the team. Address: Jukebox, H no 49, Next to Audiophile Goa, nr. मारूती मंदिर, Fontainhas (quarter), Mala, Panaji, Goa 403001, India Nutcase Etc. is a 35-seat bar that Rituparna and Avinandan Banerjee opened on the ground floor of a 109-year-old building in South Kolkata, and it sits well outside the city's usual nightlife map. The cocktails blur the line between drink and dish. Tangra Town mixes tequila with chicken broth, bell pepper and soy in a nod to chilli chicken, and a drink simply called Beer imitates the real thing in a bar that doesn't serve it. Sit at the bar and ask for seats B18 or B19, which have the best vantage point in the room. You can watch the bartenders at work and see who walks in, and since everyone in Kolkata seems to know everyone, you can also duck if you'd rather avoid small talk. Address: Ground Floor, 91, Manohar Pukur Rd, Manoharpukur, Kalighat, Kolkata, West Bengal 700029, India This article originally featured on cntraveller.in

item.title: SALES: The King Charles III England Coast Path: Where to stay along England's epic new coastal trail
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
In March 2026, HRH King Charles III climbed the chalk cliffs of the Seven Sisters in East Sussex to officially cut the ribbon on his new namesake coastal trail, a project more than a decade in the making. When fully complete (there’s no set date yet), the route will string stretches of the UK’s most beautiful corners in around 2,700 miles of coastline, making it the longest managed coastal path in the world. As of right now, more than 2,200 miles are open, with happy walkers already stomping about. In reality, that’s too much mileage to take on in one day – few walkers are likely to tackle the route end to end. So we’ve broken the route down into a few sections and called out the places to stay – from tracing Northumberland's castle-studded coastline before a session in the spa, walking across a wind-whipped stretch of Cornwall before a quiet sleep in a small fishing village or doing a spot of shopping near a groovy overnighter in Kent. These are the best places to stay on the King Charles III England Coast Path. Where to stay along the King Charles III England Coast Path The stretch closest to those setting off from London – chalky cliffs, beautiful rolling hills and squint-and-you’ll-just-see views over to France (in some areas, phones might even pick up a French signal). From the Seven Sisters and red-and-white striped Beachy Head to the White Cliffs of Dover, this is perhaps the most quintessentially English part of the coastline (and a spot that’s been seen on screen plenty). The Gallivant is a short hop from the path. It's a relaxed beach hotel (with a certain beach club feel) and it remains one of the smartest places to stay on the Sussex coast. Get lost in the beachy dunes of Camber Sands – then return for briny oysters, a glass of Kent wine and a very quiet sleep. For more local hotel recommendations, visit our guide to the best hotels in Rye. Margate's creative edge keeps sharpening. The groovy seaside town has produced no shortage of cool places to bed down (and eat), but Fort Road Hotel, the Turner Contemporary-facing place to stay, is one of the strongest (plus there is a founder of Frieze art fair connection, and some serious art on the walls). A street back from the promenade, The Rose is a colour-pop Georgian townhouse feels refreshingly down-to-earth. There are only a handful of bright rooms to snag, so planning ahead is wise. Deal's antiques and independent shops along High Street make it a charming stop for stocking up on bits to bring home. For more hotel recommendations, visit our guide to the best hotels in Kent. The coastline starts to turn a little wilder, and wider, as the path heads east where reedbeds replace cliffs, salt marshes meet vast beaches, and fishing villages swap with bird reserves and broad skies. It can be a little tougher to access by public transport, so spending a bit of extra time on either side might be a help. For more hotel recommendations, visit our guide to the best hotels in Norfolk. A short drive inland from the North Norfolk coast, The Harper – a polished conversion of a former glass-blowing factory – is a comfortable base for walkers looking to check out Wells-next-the-Sea, Blakeney and Holkham. A taxi is needed to get to and from the coast. The Suffolk is a little restaurant-with-rooms overlooking Southwold's famous pier and beach huts, with a very good whole grilled fish on the menu. The path passes practically outside the front door. Art fans adore spending a night at The Gunton Arms – a smart pub with rooms whose art collection rivals some of the world’s best museums. From Tracey Emin, Lucien Freud, Damien Hirst, Paula Rego, Gilbert and George and many more. The cliffs and blue beaches are a visual draw, of course, but there’s also a strong restaurant scene, a buzzing artists and makers movement, charming old fishing traditions (sea shanties included) and pockets of folklore that feel moody and mystical. Hope Cove House is a cheerful, 10-room hotel in one of South Devon's prettiest villages (and only 10 minutes from smart Salcombe). Several beautiful patches of the South West Coast Path are nearby, making this one of the easiest walk-and-stay combinations. For more recommendations, look to our guide to the best hotels in Devon. Hotel Tresanton, Olga Polizzi's long-standing Cornish classic still feels as stylish as when it opened its doors in 1998. Quite literally just above the water in St Mawes, it’s close enough for walking the Roseland Peninsula and some of Cornwall's less heart-pumping coastal walking. For more local recommendations, visit our guide to the best hotels in Cornwall. Overlooking Chesil Beach and the craggy Jurassic Coast, this former coaching inn, The Seaside Boarding House, has become one of the south coast's most dependable (and delicious) addresses. Bedrooms look out to sea, and the walking begins almost immediately outside, just set off after squeezing in a proper lunch. For more recommendations, look to our guide to the best hotels in Dorset. God’s own country, where big skies draw eyes from sea to star. Expect ruined abbeys, almost-empty beaches, fishing villages and castles peeking out at the North Sea. It also remains one of the quieter stretches of the whole country, with long walks between villages and most certainly fewer crowds than Cornwall. For more recommendations, visit our guide to the best hotels in Yorkshire. One of the most exciting recent hotel openings on the Yorkshire coast over the past few years, Saltmoore mixes North Sea access with smart interiors, good food and a serious wellness space. Fish and chips in Whitby and Robin Hood's Bay are not far either. Set within a former convent in the centre of Alnwick, The Cookie Jar is sweet hotel is a short drive from some of the most spectacular sections of the path, including Bamburgh Castle and the beaches around Holy Island. Pop into Barter Books – a packed-to-the-brim bookshop inside a former Victorian train station – for some reading while you sit for a break from the walking.

item.title: SALES: Boating Is a Notorious Money Pit. This Club Wants to Change That.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Two things about me are true: I love spending time boating, and I’ll never own a boat. Despite how much I love to parade atop the water, I don’t see boat ownership through rose-colored glasses—it’s a notorious money pit. Boating has always had a high barrier to entry that other outdoor pursuits don’t: you can rent a kayak or SUP for an afternoon, but a motorized boat has usually meant a dock of sorts, a trailer, a license, and a five-figure commitment before you’ve even revved the engine. Sailboats, while glamorous, are even worse. Clubs like Freedom Boat Club, now with roughly 450 locations across the US, Europe, Australia, New Zealand, and the Middle East, are trying to lower that barrier. Treating access to the water less like a purchase and more like a gym membership. An estimated 100 million Americans get out on the water every year, but only about 150,000 new boats are sold. That’s the gap this membership is attempting to bridge: people who want to boat, but never saw a realistic way in. Freedom Boat Club operates like a timeshare, with some key differences. The first being that there are a lot fewer strings involved, and also, no free conference room lunch. To join the club, there’s an initiation fee of around $5,000 and then additional monthly fees of around $500. Membership includes access to a fleet of over 5,000 boats, and after a few mandatory introductory courses on safety and operation, members may rent boats anywhere, at any time. That means snowbirds can boat all summer long off of Long Island, then flee down south without missing a single day on the water. Or, a bride-to-be can take her bachelorette crew out on Lake Austin, no scammy boat rental needed. Up to four reservations can be booked at a time, each for around three to four hours, and yes, double booking is allowed so you can enjoy the whole day on the water. Aside from a few popular water days (think Fourth of July or Labor Day Weekend), boats typically don’t need to be reserved more than a few days out, and to date, around 670,000 trips are booked a year. The boats themselves are leased through Brunswick Boat Club (the parent company of Freedom Boat Club), and include myriad styles for all types of outdoor activities: smooth Boston Whalers and pontoons perfect for family trips, zippy bow riders, inshore or offshore boats perfect for fishing, sailboats and plenty more. Some of the boats require additional training, but as Will Sangster, the President of Business Acceleration at Freedom Boat Club, tells me, it’s only about 10 percent of the fleet. Best of all, the boats are new. The club cycles out boats after about three years, so you won’t be getting any sort of water jalopy. Of the roughly 400 locations in the U.S., the club occupies space in a variety of waters: open ocean, lakes, rivers, bays, so wherever you want to get outside, there’s a boat to help you do it. The idea of getting more people out on the water is the central message for Freedom Boat Club. In fact, the club aims to bring a new wave (pun intended) of boaters to the scene. The club’s membership base is clustered in the late 30s to mid-40s, much younger than traditional boat ownership, which is somewhere between the 60s and 70s, according to the National Marine Manufacturers Association. Roughly four out of every 10 members of the club are new to boating altogether, and according to Brenna Preisser, the President of Brunswick Boat Club, women make up nearly 30 percent of the club’s membership compared to around 12 percent of traditional boat ownership. For me, reading a book under the sun while gently bobbing on the deck of a pontoon on a lake in Upstate, New York is as close to utopia as I’ll ever get. What I love most about that feeling is how nothing feels so big or scary out on the water—it’s as close to a moment of pure peace as I’m capable of having. As much as I love it, boat ownership is not for me. The maintenance, fuel, docking, and storage fees amount to a bill I never want to see. What I yearn for is far simpler: the open water, sunshine, a fresh breeze, and of course, my book sitting on my chest, dog-eared. No room for the angst of individual boat ownership or the vague hope of getting an invite onto a friend’s boat. Instead, I’m just a reservation, and a few intro to boating courses, away from my perfect summer day.

item.title: SALES: Canned Vegetables Have a Bad Reputation. These Trail-Friendly, Pocket-Sized Tins Are Changing That.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
At the southern end of Idaho’s Teton Valley, just over the pass from Jackson Hole and adjacent to some world-class fly-fishing, sits an unassuming little structure stocked floor to ceiling with delicious things. At Food Shed Idaho, specialty grocer Cecily Costa helps her customers provision their outdoor adventures. Something she’s excited about right now: petite Sweet Prince tomatoes. They come in a tin slim enough to slip in your pocket—a game changer in itself. “Tomatoes generally don’t travel well for hikes or picnics,” Costa says. “I think these are going to do very well.” The tins are new this year from Row 7 Seed Company, chef Dan Barber’s clap back to commodity-vegetable breeding, which prioritizes traits like yield and shipability over flavor. And vegetable quality begins with the seed. “Even the organic vegetables you eat in this country come mostly from conventional seed, produced with chemical interventions,” Barber says. “We choose to start with organic seed. It produces a stronger, more delicious plant—and, we think, a more nutrient-dense one. We’re working on putting some science behind that last point, but the early indications are incredible.” Row 7 seeks out innovative breeders using traditional cross-pollination and selection to develop flavorful new cultivars. Then the company partners with farmers it trusts to do justice to that breeding in the way they raise the produce, sold at Whole Foods and other grocers. Row 7 also sells its seeds in packets and, now, three of its flavor-forward varieties ready to eat, in chic little tins. There’s that Sweet Prince, tinned at peak summer sweetness with a balancing, racy acidity. The Sweet Garleek, a garlic-leek hybrid, comes confited in extra-virgin olive oil, white balsamic vinegar, and Dijon mustard—“like leeks vinaigrette with the volume turned up,” says Row 7 co-founder Charlotte Douglas. And I have never tasted another beet remotely like the Badger Flame. That earthy flavor so many people don’t care for? Gone. This beet has a bright, surprising taste to match its golden color and comes in succulent little cubes you can toss into a salad, or snack on straight from the tin. Row 7’s slender tins are portable and adorable—distinct, crucially, from the shape of can we associate with lank green beans. And the brand no doubt benefits from the cachet the format has acquired with the tinned-fish trend in recent years. But Douglas emphasizes the culinary benefits. “The format follows the function, really,” she explains. “A smaller tin size allows us more control over the cooking process. And we do think about it like cooking, not like processing. How do we best preserve flavor and texture?” This kind of care applied to a canned vegetable may be something new in American grocery stores, but the practice of tinning certain treasured varieties during their fleeting weeks of peak ripeness has a long history in Spain (where eating fresh produce out of season might as well be illegal). I can think of no better example of this type of conserva than the “Cojonudos” White Asparagus from the Navarra-based company El Navarrico. Cojonudos translates as “awesome,” and that’s the word for these fat spears of white asparagus tinned with nothing more than water and salt. Navarran farmers tenderly mound dirt on the plants in early spring to prevent photosynthesis and the bitter vegetal edge that comes with it. The pale spears have an irresistible, nutty flavor that’s delicious straight from the can—as is the brine, infused with the essence of the vegetable and a way tastier source of electrolytes than Gatorade. (It also does wonders for a vinaigrette.) You really shouldn’t let a drop of the brine or oil from any good conserva go to waste, if you ask Nacho Valle. When he was growing up in Valencia and working in the orange groves, “the workers were always opening tins. They have a piece of bread, they dunk the bread in the tin and they eat it.” After Valle moved to New York City, he and three Spanish friends would regularly gather over tins of fish or vegetable conservas, some bread or potato chips, and Spanish vermouth. In 2021, the four friends founded Lata (Spanish for “tin”) to sell their favorite tinned products; now they import them, too. Lata’s online store carries the largest selection of plant-based conservas I’ve found anywhere. From Porto-Muiños, a family-owned outfit in Galicia that sustainably harvests edible seaweed, the Tapa of Piquillo Peppers with Sweet Kombu delivers an intense umami flavor to complement the sweetness of the tender red peppers. The Codium is a seaweed with a satisfying bite and a clean, briny flavor that make it a nice alternative to caviar. Lata also stocks the smoky Celery Root Whitefish from Canadian brand Seed to Surf, another plant-based product that gets a savory taste of the ocean from seaweed. My favorite way to serve all of the above is the Spanish way, right in the tin, with potato chips for scooping. The classic Galician brand Bonilla a la Vista is the chip for that: olive-oil-fried, delicately crisp, just salty enough. The best part? They, too, come in tins. Umami from the seaweed makes a perfect pair for the pepper’s sweetness. Grab potato chips and scoop right into the sustainably harvested, delicate, velvety seaweed for a briny caviar substitute. Fat, nutty spears of white asparagus grown in Navarra, Spain, packed in water and salt. No earthy funk in these golden beets. Toss the bright cubes into salads or apps, or eat straight from the tin. Seed to Surf has managed to make a flaky, smoky plant-based alternative to whitefish. This article is from the Fall 2026 issue of Outside magazine. item.title: REVIEW: Webex by Cisco Review: Dependable Video Meetings With Robust Collaboration Tools
item.description:
Source: PCMag
As one of the most established video conferencing platforms on the market, Cisco's Webex Meetings serves as the reliable anchor of the broader Webex Suite. Beyond dependable calling and team messaging, the platform stands out with an intuitive digital whiteboard and Vidcast, an integrated asynchronous video tool. While its built-in AI Assistant handles real-time questions and meeting recaps cleanly, Cisco still trails Zoom Workplace in deeper agentic productivity, though significant updates are slated for early 2027. Thanks to its stability, expansive enterprise capabilities, and aggressive pricing that undercuts key rivals, Webex by Cisco earns our Editors' Choice award alongside Zoom. With a free Webex account, you can host an unlimited number of meetings of up to 40 minutes and with up to 100 participants. Free users get up to 720p video quality, along with breakout rooms, local meeting recording, reactions, screen sharing, virtual backgrounds, and unlimited whiteboards. This version also supports audio calls between Webex accounts, text chat, and video messages. Thankfully, you can sign up without providing a credit card. The Webex Meet ($12 per user per month, billed annually) and Suite ($22.50 per user per month, billed annually) plans increase the meeting time limit to 24 hours, and the participant limit to 200. They also unlock 10GB of cloud space for encrypted meeting recordings, 1080p video, Cisco’s AI Assistant (which can catch you up on meetings and generate summaries of them, among other things), closed captions with highlights, and live polling. The Webex Suite plan notably adds VoIP features, including a business phone number, outgoing phone service, and visual voicemail. I didn't test the VoIP functionality for this review. The company also sells a Webex Enterprise plan (custom pricing) that adds more call management features, allows meetings with up to 1,000 participants, and unlocks unlimited local and cloud recording. For webinars, you need the Webex Webinar plan, which starts at $56.25 per user per month (billed annually) and supports unlimited webinars with up to 1,000 viewers. Webex also sells a real-time translation add-on that can translate speech between over 100 different languages; it costs $300 per license per year. A Call Me add-on lets Webex call you at a phone number you choose to join a meeting’s audio; it costs $48 per license per year for domestic calls to Canada and the US, or $429 per license per year for international calls to numbers in 70 countries. Webex's base paid plan is an excellent value relative to its competitors. For comparison, Google Meet’s Business Standard edition costs $14 per user per month (billed annually) for up to 150 participants, while Zoom Workplace costs $14.16 per user per month for meetings with up to 100 participants. Webex’s free plan is reasonable, although it has an inconvenient 40-minute maximum meeting length, a limitation it shares with Zoom Workplace’s free plan. Google Meet’s free plan lets you have one-on-one calls for up to 24 hours and limits group calls to 60 minutes, making it a better choice for longer meetings. You can sign up for a free Webex account on Cisco’s website; all you need is an email address. Dedicated apps are available for Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, and Windows, and the web version is compatible with all major web browsers. Cisco recently announced a new Webex app experience with deeper AI integrations and agentic features, and says it should arrive in the first quarter of 2027. I look forward to testing it once it's live. After signing in, the current Webex desktop app opens to the Meetings view, where you can schedule and view upcoming meetings. The mobile and web versions work similarly. You can connect Webex to a Google Calendar or Microsoft 365 calendar, or you can use Webex’s native scheduling features. Webex gives each user a Personal Room; people who want to chat with you can join via a persistent link. The Meetings experience is highly intuitive. Before joining a meeting, the app shows a preview screen where you can configure audio and video devices. You can also invite people to your meeting or copy a link to share with others so they can join from a web browser (even if they don’t have a Webex account). The meetings view has a streamlined interface with common options visible on the toolbar, and less common settings appearing under a More Options menu. The app supports standard features, including emoji reactions, hand raises, recording, and screen sharing. A Layout button lets you control how the meeting participants’ video feeds are organized. Webex has a comprehensive online support portal that includes the Cisco AI Assistant, which can search the company's documentation to answer your questions. I asked how to enable end-to-end encryption for meetings, for example, and the AI Assistant provided detailed instructions. It's a useful tool. Free users have to make do with just the online help center, but paid subscribers can get support via chat, phone, or case forms. During East Coast business hours, I was able to reach a representative via the online chat feature within a few seconds. Cisco also advertises dedicated representatives for Webex Enterprise users. To start, Webex integrates with Google Calendar and Microsoft Outlook to schedule meetings. Otherwise, the Webex App Hub integrates with hundreds of business tools, including Notion, Salesforce, Slack, and Zendesk. Webex also has MCP servers that organizations can use to find messages, schedule meetings, and perform other tasks via chatbots such as Claude. I tested Webex by Cisco on an Android phone, an iPad, a MacBook, and a Windows 11 PC, and the experience felt stable across all of them, with smooth video quality. Anecdotally, I’ve used Webex for various meetings over the last 15 years, and I’ve consistently had a stable experience, even in meetings with hundreds of participants. The Webex Free plan tops out at 720p video quality, but that’s also true for paid Webex plans in many situations. Cisco says Webex uses 720p video by default, although administrators can enable 1080p for their organizations. Webex beats Zoom on out-of-the-box video quality, however, since the latter defaults to 360p unless an admin activates 720p. I would still prefer it if Webex just made 1080p the default for everyone. Google Meet supports 1080p with no extra configuration required, as does Apple’s free FaceTime. Intermedia AnyMeeting lags behind the others, with video quality that tops out at 720p. Cisco provided an account with 1080p video already active for my review, and I didn't experience any performance issues in testing. Note that the app automatically lowers video quality to maintain smooth streaming performance under challenging network conditions. For screen sharing, Webex promises up to 5K resolution. When I screen-shared from a 4K Windows desktop, text was legible, and images looked sharp. Paid Webex plans support closed captions in English, French, German, and Spanish, and this feature worked well in testing. All you have to do is specify the spoken and caption languages. Captions appeared quickly and seemed accurate when I tried translating my English speech into French. As mentioned, translation features for additional languages require a paid add-on. Both capabilities can be invaluable for meetings with international participants. Beyond business communication features, Webex by Cisco includes an AI assistant, AI meeting recaps, a video-sharing service, and a whiteboard tool. AI Assistant: Informative In-Meeting Answers The Webex Meetings interface shows a status icon when the Cisco AI Assistant is transcribing a meeting. In addition to viewing a full transcript after a meeting concludes, you can ask the AI Assistant about a meeting's content while it's happening. The AI Assistant didn't have any issues answering questions about recent topics under discussion. If you don't want to use the AI Assistant at all, you can simply click the Stop AI button. Zoom Workplace's AI features do all of this and much more. For example, it offers AI-powered productivity tools for creating and editing documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and emails. Cisco says it’s launching more agentic functionality in Webex in the first quarter of 2027, as mentioned, so Webex might close the gap soon. Meeting Summaries and Transcripts: Convenient, Automated Record-Keeping Webex shows details for past recorded meetings in the Meetings pane. You can click a meeting to view a complete transcript with identified speakers, for example, as well as read an AI-generated executive summary of said meeting. The summaries and transcripts were accurate and useful in my testing. Webex lets everyone collaborate on an unlimited number of whiteboards. You can access whiteboards during meetings or via the Whiteboard section of the app. The tool lets you draw freely and insert images, text, and emoji. It’s a comprehensive set of capabilities, but Zoom Workplace again goes further by supporting AI-driven creation of whiteboard layouts. Vidcast: Compelling Video Messages Outside Meetings The Webex Suite includes Cisco’s easy-to-use Vidcast service, even for free users. It lets you record video messages and turn moments from meetings into recorded messages, using AI to edit the video and extract highlights. You can also trim and edit videos yourself using the provided editing tools. Cisco pitches Vidcast’s video messages as a time-saving alternative to meetings and a more genuine alternative to text messages. I found creating a video message easy, and the AI highlights feature did a good job of editing the video into a short, shareable clip. Beyond meetings, Webex supports 1:1 audio and video calls, as well as messaging. When you receive an incoming call, you can accept it easily. The call interface is a simplified version of the meeting experience without features such as the AI assistant, breakout rooms, closed captions, and whiteboards. As mentioned, the Webex Suite plan extends this feature with outgoing phone calls, a phone number for incoming calls, voicemail, and other business VoIP functionality. The platform supports standard team chat features, including direct messages, emoji responses, spaces, and threads, so it could be sufficient for organizations standardizing on Webex. This functionality works as expected, and I was able to chat with a Webex user outside my organization. Unlike Zoom Workplace, the Webex Suite can’t bring your email into a unified inbox. Cisco says Webex communication always happens over encrypted channels to secure your meetings. The company publishes detailed security and privacy information. Webex also supports zero-trust security for optional end-to-end encryption for confidential meetings, which ensures even Webex employees can't see the content of your organization’s meetings. Administrators can require multi-factor authentication for everyone. Cisco also provides administrators with data residency controls, enabling organizations to use data centers in their preferred geographic areas. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Webex by Cisco delivers enterprise-grade video conferencing paired with reliable stability and straightforward usability. Beyond meetings, the broader Webex Suite shines through polished cross-platform apps, dependable team messaging, and Vidcast asynchronous video. While its AI capabilities trail Zoom Workplace's more robust productivity ecosystem, Webex counters with aggressive pricing, a generous free tier, and an expansive feature set. For organizations seeking dependable collaboration without a steep price tag, Webex by Cisco earns our Editors' Choice award.
